justification: A single human study (PMID 32573102) reports a homozygous MRVI1/IRAG1 mutation in a family with non-syndromic isolated achalasia, which is credible but not replicated in independent probands or families, so "Established" cannot be supported (only one qualifying PMID). Strong supporting biology exists: IRAG1 is a key component of the NO/cGMP/cGKI signaling complex controlling smooth muscle relaxation, including human colonic smooth muscle cells, which is the exact mechanism impaired in achalasia (PMIDs 11309393, 21865585, 12480535, 16166082). A microRNA–mRNA network study in achalasia patients (PMID 31773868) may add indirect human transcriptomic support. Other papers concern platelet reactivity, moyamoya syndrome, murine leukemia integration sites, or HCN4 channel regulation and do not bear on achalasia causality. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" since much of the supporting data is functional/in vitro.

Three independent human genetic reports present their own patient-derived ADAMTS9 variants in ciliopathy: PMID 30609407 identified biallelic ADAMTS9 mutations (c.4575_4576del, c.194C>G) in families with nephronophthisis-related ciliopathy with supporting functional and zebrafish data; PMID 34750010 reported compound heterozygous ADAMTS9 variants in Joubert syndrome-related disorders; and PMID 37035301 described novel compound heterozygous variants in two siblings with ADAMTS9-related nephropathy/NPHP-RC modeled in kidney organoids. A curated ACMG-based review of ADAMTS family Mendelian disease (PMID 32183147) independently classifies ADAMTS9 as strongly associated with nephronophthisis-related ciliopathy. Mechanistic work showing ADAMTS9 cleaves the MKS protein TMEM67 to control transition-zone assembly (PMIDs 39282264, 40436881, 41542618), including functional analysis of all eight reported patient variants, further corroborates causality. Remaining probability reflects the modest number of reported probands, which some might view as limited rather than definitive replication.

SLC34A1 is firmly established as a human disease gene for phosphate-wasting tubulopathies (idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia type 2, hypophosphatemic nephrolithiasis), with multiple patient cohorts carrying biallelic and monoallelic variants (PMID 26047794, 29924459, 39461557, 41543768, 40943461). For the specific entity "Fanconi renotubular syndrome 2," however, the primary evidence rests on a single small family originally reported outside this list, and reviews here explicitly caution that this gene–disease association is doubtful because the implicated in-frame deletion (91del7) is common in population databases (PMID 33283647, 38042745). Within the provided literature, patient-level results showing a proximal Fanconi-type phenotype attributable to SLC34A1 are limited largely to PMID 29924459 (mixed phenotype with metabolic acidosis and hyperphosphaturia) and descriptive series listing FRTS2 as part of the phenotypic spectrum (PMID 41543768), which is insufficient for independent replication of the classic Fanconi syndrome phenotype. Since generalized/partial proximal tubular dysfunction and renal phosphate wasting are mechanistically and clinically linked subtypes of the SLC34A1 spectrum, "Existing" best captures the evidence, with meaningful residual probability for "Established."

Multiple independent human studies report SPTAN1 variants in patients with spastic paraplegia: PMID 35150594 describes de novo and dominantly inherited SPTAN1 variants causing spastic paraplegia with cerebellar ataxia in several families, PMID 40397273 characterizes a recurrent SPTAN1 mutation causing SPG91 (the formally designated HSP locus), and PMID 36331550 expands the monoallelic phenotype to include pure spastic paraplegia. Additional independent probands support a recessive form: PMID 31515523 (two biallelic patients from an HSP cohort) and PMID 34526651 (a consanguineous family with homozygous p.I1388V and complicated HSP), with a further case in PMID 41338915. These are patient-based genetic findings in humans, replicated across unrelated probands and supported by a recognized OMIM designation (SPG91), rather than mere background citations. Remaining probability is assigned to "Existing" to account for phenotypic heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding some recessive variant reports.

Only one article (PMID 20071345) provides direct human genetic evidence: linkage mapping in extended TAPVR kindreds plus mutation analysis implicating PDGFRA in total anomalous pulmonary venous return, a bona fide congenital heart defect, supported by chick and mouse knockdown models reproducing inflow tract anomalies. This is a single study without independent replication, so it does not meet the bar for "Established" (which would require at least two independent reports of patient variants). The remaining papers concern gastrointestinal stromal tumor syndromes, gliomas, and orofacial clefting, and are not evidence for cardiac phenotypes; the MUTYH/glioma papers are essentially incidental co-mentions. Given the credible but limited human evidence combined with strong supporting developmental biology, "Existing" is the best fit, with some residual probability on "Hypothesized" if one weights the animal-model component more heavily.

Direct human genetic evidence exists: Gauthier et al. (PMID 20385823) reported two de novo SHANK3 point mutations (R1117X, R536W) in two independent schizophrenia families ascertained for the disorder, the basis for the SCZD15 designation. A targeted resequencing study (PMID 28371232) identified rare functional variants (notably p.G1011V, seen in several SCZ cases and absent in sequenced controls) but failed to confirm association for the common variants tested, so replication is suggestive rather than definitive. Additional supporting but weaker human data come from genotype–phenotype reviews of SHANK3 de novo mutations listing schizophrenia among outcomes (PMID 30537371) and from Phelan-McDermid cohorts where psychiatric diagnoses including schizophrenia occur, though those largely involve multigene deletions and therefore cannot isolate SHANK3. Given one clear de novo mutation study plus one partially supportive rare-variant study, the evidence sits between Existing and Established, weighted toward Existing.

Several human studies report point (non-CNV) LAS1L variants in independent probands with syndromic X-linked intellectual disability phenotypes: the X-exome sequencing study of 405 XLID families listed LAS1L among validated novel XLID genes with co-segregating variants (PMID 25644381); an independent cohort with a Lujan-Fryns-like XLID phenotype identified a private LAS1L mutation in one patient (PMID 26358559); an Angelman-like WES cohort reported an X-linked pathogenic LAS1L variant (PMID 34653234); and a recent case describes a novel hemizygous frameshift (c.2082dup) with functional testing, expanding the Wilson-Turner syndrome spectrum (PMID 42353867). Additional human reports link LAS1L to allelic severe infantile neuromuscular/SMARD-like disease (PMIDs 24647030, 35627110), and mechanistic work on Las1L in ribosome biogenesis supports biological plausibility (PMIDs 28652339, 31288032, 32220933). Replication across independent probands with single-gene variants supports Established, though several reports are single cases with variable phenotypes and limited functional segregation data, leaving meaningful weight on Existing.

phenotype: intellectual disability, anterior maxillary protrusion, and strabismus
justification: Only one article in this set reports human variant-level evidence: PMID 21035105, which identified a truncating SOBP mutation segregating in a single consanguineous family with mental retardation, anterior maxillary protrusion and strabismus (MRAMS) syndrome plus a nonsyndromic ID case. That is a single family/report, so replication in independent probands is not demonstrated here, which caps the evidence at "Existing." Supporting biological plausibility comes from non-human work: the mouse Jxc1/Sobp mutant with cochlear patterning defects (PMID 18579736), Xenopus studies showing Sobp acts as a Six1/Eya cofactor in craniofacial and otic development (PMIDs 34414417, 42475796, 37830236), and fish jaw-deformity association (PMID 27929136); these are animal/in vitro and thus contribute to "Hypothesized" rather than human evidence. Other listed papers (methylome study, blood pressure, intervertebral disc microarray) are incidental co-mentions.

The original SPG43 locus was mapped in a Malian family (PMID 20039086) and the causal gene identified by exome sequencing as C19orf12 with a homozygous p.Ala63Pro variant in the affected sisters, with functional confirmation of mislocalization (PMID 23857908). Independent replication with patient-level variant data comes from a second family with compound heterozygous C19orf12 variants (c.204_214del, c.32C>T) presenting an SPG43 phenotype in one sib and an ALS-like phenotype in the other (PMID 33394258), and an additional case of C19orf12-related disease presenting as spastic paraparesis/SPG43 (PMID 34298215). Allelism with MPAN is well documented (PMIDs 31804703, 39755877), and SPG43 is a recognized allelic phenotype of C19orf12 without brain iron accumulation. A negative screening cohort (PMID 26714052) shows the subtype is rare but does not contradict causality; some residual probability is kept for "Existing" because SPG43-specific reports remain few.

The original mapping and gene identification study (PMID 20624953) reported a 5'UTR regulatory variant (c.-172G>A) segregating in the AUNA1 family with functional evidence of DIAPH3 overexpression, plus Drosophila corroboration. Independent human families with distinct variants have since been reported: PMID 27658576 (c.-173C>T in a dominant auditory neuropathy family), PMID 42345014 (a 5' regulatory structural variant segregating with postlingual hearing loss/auditory neuropathy in a multigenerational Brazilian family), and PMID 40040362 (de novo p.Glu137Asp with auditory neuropathy spectrum phenotype), with an additional family in PMID 41511813. These are independent probands/families with single-gene-level variants, satisfying replication. Mouse (diap3 transgenic, PMID 28058271) and review literature (PMIDs 35681420, 34685534) provide supporting mechanistic evidence but are not the primary basis for the Established call.

The TRIM69-specific literature is functional/virological: TRIM69 is an interferon-stimulated gene that restricts vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus (PMID 31375575) and acts as a pantropic viral inhibitor via microtubule regulation in IFN-stimulated myeloid cells (PMID 36251989), plus developmental roles in zebrafish (PMIDs 27050765, 27031046) and a mitotic role (PMID 37739411). No article reports pathogenic germline TRIM69 variants in patients with infectious susceptibility; the only human population genetic observation is signatures of positive selection, and the HIV/HCV study (PMID 29269866) reports DNA methylation, not genetic variation, so it cannot support "Existing." The remaining papers (TRIF/RIPK1/NFKB1/IRAK2/WWP2/N4BP1/TRIM56) concern other genes and are irrelevant homolog/pathway co-mentions. Thus the evidence supports a biologically plausible, mechanistically grounded but genetically unproven relationship: Hypothesized.

The decisive evidence is a single study (PMID 21907016) reporting linkage to 6p22.1 and an exome-identified missense variant (c.398C>G) in MOG segregating in one large multiplex narcolepsy-with-cataplexy family, absent in 775 controls, with supporting in vitro mislocalization data — this defines narcolepsy 7. That is credible human genetic evidence but comes from one family/proband set, with the functional confirmation performed in mouse oligodendrocytes rather than replicated clinical cohorts. PMID 25197808 searched for rare variants in HLA-DQB1*06:02-negative hypocretin-deficient narcolepsy but does not provide clear independent replication of pathogenic MOG variants, and PMID 17256150 examined MOG microsatellite markers mainly in an MS context, finding predisposing effects in MS but not narcolepsy families. All remaining articles concern MOG antibody-associated demyelinating disease, MOGAD/NMOSD, or EAE models and are irrelevant to narcolepsy genetics. Because I cannot cite two independent human studies with disease-causing MOG variants, the evidence supports "Existing" rather than "Established."

Two human reports provide primary variant-level evidence: PMID 21212097 identified a homozygous TECR p.P182L variant segregating in five affected siblings of a consanguineous family with non-syndromic ARID, and PMID 35709344 reported an independent proband (outside the original sibship) homozygous for the same c.545C>T Hutterite founder variant, expanding the phenotype. Functional work in human cells (PMID 24220030) demonstrates that P182L reduces trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase activity/stability and alters sphingolipid profiles, supporting causality mechanistically. Points are withheld from full certainty because the two reports involve the same founder mutation in the same restricted population, and other listed articles (PMID 22419660 multigene 19p13 deletion; PMID 24040793, 27012031) only cite the association as background. Animal/cell studies (PMIDs 35465346, 41415402, 42323083) support relevant biology but do not add human genetic replication.

Human evidence exists but is thin: a single Kuwaiti family with reported novel CRYGB mutations in autosomal dominant congenital cataract (PMID 23288985), plus association/polymorphism studies of CRYGA/CRYGB variants and a CRYGB promoter variant (G-47A) in cataract patients (PMIDs 21941057, 26552302). Crucially, the formal ClinGen-style curation of crystallin genes classified CRYGB as only "Limited," noting essentially absent clinical evidence and reliance on experimental data (PMID 42091610), which precludes an "Established" call since I cannot cite two independent, convincing proband/family reports. Much of the supporting evidence is non-human: mouse Crygb mutants (Cat2nop, Clapper gammaB-I4F) and canine/feline candidate-gene studies that actually excluded CRYGB (PMIDs 9782080, 15878859, 10627821, 17327821, 35205377, 20423916), which supports biological plausibility rather than human causality. Several other listed papers merely include CRYGB in screening panels without positive findings (PMIDs 22669729, 37048143). Therefore the weight sits on "Existing," with substantial residual probability for "Hypothesized."

The only available article (PMID: 33981260) is a Drosophila study of dPECR (peroxisomal trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase) in the context of ethanol reconsumption preference and neuroprotection against oxidative stress — an invertebrate model of alcohol use disorder, not a human neurodevelopmental disorder. No human genetic variants, probands, or families linking PECR to neurodevelopmental disorder are reported, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded. There is a weak biological thread (neuronal protection against oxidative stress in neurons upon dPECR loss) that could be construed as tangentially relevant to neural function, supporting a modest allocation to Hypothesized. However, the phenotype studied (ethanol consumption preference) is a substance-use behavior rather than a neurodevelopmental phenotype, so the co-mention is largely incidental, favoring Novel.

No article reports point/sequence variants in ARL14EP causing a neurodevelopmental disorder in independent probands, so Established is untenable. The strongest human-genomic hints are indirect: WAGR syndrome patients with multigene 11p13 deletions that include ARL14EP (PMID 36011342), where the gene was implicated only in lens abnormalities and the deletion cannot single out this gene, and a CSV/genome-first study listing the ARL14EP-DT/FSHB locus as a candidate within a cohort including neurodevelopmental genomic disorders (PMID 42410935) — suggestive but not definitive. A cross-trait psychiatric/reproductive GWAS implicates ARL14EP in an endometriosis–bipolar disorder link (PMID 41578317), a psychiatric rather than clearly neurodevelopmental phenotype, giving modest support to Existing. The most compelling mechanistic rationale is non-human: the C. elegans orthologue ARLE-14 partners with MET-2/SETDB1 to time heterochromatin formation during embryogenesis (PMID 30140741), a chromatin-regulation pathway strongly tied to chromatinopathies and NDDs, favoring Hypothesized; the remaining literature (PCOS TWAS, infertility GWAS, pig vaccine GWAS) is phenotypically unrelated, leaving some weight on Novel.

Only one article (PMID 40241305) provides human genetic evidence: a pan-histonopathy cohort in which a single previously unpublished individual carried a germline variant in HIST3H3/H3-4, a gene explicitly described as "not previously associated with disease." This is a single proband without replication in independent families, so it cannot meet the bar for Established. The remaining literature concerns H3.4/H3t biology in spermatogenesis, nucleosome instability, chaperone interactions, and PTMs in mice and in vitro (e.g., PMIDs 28099840, 20498094, 42248887, 41980770), which supports chromatin-related biological plausibility but not a neurodevelopmental phenotype; those would only support Hypothesized. Given the credible but singular human report within a well-characterized histonopathy framework, Existing is the most probable designation, with residual weight on Hypothesized if the single case is judged insufficient.

The only primary human genetic evidence in this set is Ngeow/Orloff et al. (PMID 23246288), which reported two germline AKT1 mutations in 91 PTEN-negative Cowden/Cowden-like probands with supporting functional data (increased P-Thr308-AKT, elevated PIP3) — this directly underlies the OMIM designation "Cowden syndrome 6." Other supportive items (PMID 24206815, a commentary/review on those same germline PIK3CA/AKT1 findings; PMID 26120150, a case report/review stating AKT1 among CS-causing genes) restate the association as background rather than providing independent proband-level replication. Additional AKT1 papers concern Proteus syndrome (PMID 30103035, 38074478), somatic tumor or signaling biology, or unrelated phenotypes, which are only mechanistically related (PI3K/AKT hyperactivation) and do not constitute Cowden-specific evidence. Because I can cite only one primary study with variants identified in Cowden patients, the evidence is credible but not replicated, favoring "Existing" over "Established."

Human variant-level evidence exists in independent probands: Kuo et al. reported two missense SEPT12 mutations (p.Thr89Met, p.Asp197Asn) in infertile men with defective sperm annulus (PMID 22275165), a novel T96I mutation was found in an infertile man with head/annulus defects (PMID 39850804), a missense c.673C>A was identified in a man with non-obstructive azoospermia (PMID 30488758), and c.474G>A was associated with teratozoospermia and truncated protein (PMID 22479503, 31880374, 34057684). Case-control SNP studies in Japanese SCOS and meiotic-arrest azoospermia patients add association-level support (PMIDs 21636737, 22116646). However, the evidence is not definitive: a recent curated gene-panel reassessment classified SEPTIN12 gene–disease validity as only "limited" (PMID 38664359), and mouse work showed haploinsufficiency does not cause infertility, undermining the heterozygous dominant model on which several human reports rest (PMID 35547809). Supporting biology (annulus filament formation, SUN4/LAMINB1 complexes) is strong but mostly functional/animal, so "Existing" is the best fit with meaningful probability for "Established."

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic NDUFA12 variants in patients with Leigh syndrome: PMID 21617257 first described a girl with Leigh syndrome and isolated complex I deficiency caused by an NDUFA12 mutation; PMID 33715266 reported seven patients from four unrelated families with novel homozygous NDUFA12 variants, six presenting with Leigh syndrome; PMID 35141356 characterized additional biallelic loss-of-function cases spanning Leigh/Leigh-like syndrome to isolated optic atrophy. Further reports and a published exchange on phenotypic heterogeneity (PMIDs 34888984, 34888988, 39819107, 41694149) corroborate the association in independent probands, and cell/mouse work (PMID 32335026) provides mechanistic support. These constitute replicated, human, single-gene evidence (not multi-gene CNVs), so the relationship is Established.

phenotype: hemolytic uremic syndrome, atypical, susceptibility to, 1
justification: The bulk of the human evidence linking CFHR3 to aHUS comes from the homozygous/heterozygous CFHR3-CFHR1 deletion associated with anti-Factor H autoantibody aHUS (DEAP-HUS) (PMID 18006700, 31118930, 35405682, 24249282), but this is a multigene copy-number variant that cannot isolate CFHR3 from CFHR1 — indeed, PMID 19745068 showed that isolated CFHR1 deficiency, not CFHR3 deficiency, correlates with anti-FH antibodies. A hybrid CFH/CFHR3 gene arising from a microhomology-mediated deletion was described in one aHUS family with functional characterization (PMID 22058112), and a single case report describes a homozygous CFHR3 deletion (PMID 39184759), but these are again structural rearrangements and single families. Large statistical analyses of rare variants (PMID 29500241) found significant enrichment only in CFH, CFI, CD46, C3, and DGKE — not CFHR3. Thus there is credible, replicated human association evidence placing CFHR3 within a disease-associated locus and risk haplotype, but no two independent reports of CFHR3-specific point variants causing aHUS, so "Existing" is the best fit, with some residual probability for "Established" given the widespread clinical acceptance of the CFHR3-CFHR1 deletion as a susceptibility factor.

The only primary human genetic study here is "Analysis of FOXD3 sequence variation in human ocular disease" (PMID 22815627), which specifically screened FOXD3 in anterior segment dysgenesis/ocular disease patients on the rationale of its neural crest role; this is a single, limited report rather than replicated causal proof. Two reviews (PMID 30100922, 35791108) restate FOXD3 as implicated in aniridia-like/ASD phenotypes "in isolated studies," which is background citation rather than independent evidence, and explicitly note only isolated reports. Strong supporting biology exists but is non-human: zebrafish foxd3 is required for neural crest specification and periocular mesenchyme contribution to the anterior segment (PMIDs 32528955, 16499899, 28681995, 36278547), and mouse Foxd3 acts in cardiac/cranial neural crest (PMID 21254333). Several other papers concern melanoma, GIST, lymphoma or vitiligo and are irrelevant to ASD. Therefore Existing is most probable, with substantial weight on Hypothesized if the single human report is considered non-definitive, and Established is unsupported since fewer than two independent human proband studies demonstrate causation.

The provided list contains no primary human genetic study whose own results identify FUS variants in essential tremor probands or families; the ETM4 link (FUS p.Q290X in a large ET kindred) appears only as background in reviews (PMID 24840975, 32307925), which counts as citation rather than replication. A screening study in the list explicitly concluded that FUS variants are not a common cause of PD or ET (PMID 24262168), indicating limited/unreplicated evidence. The bulk of the remaining literature concerns FUS in ALS/FTD, phase separation, DNA repair, and therapeutic silencing—mechanistically relevant but not ET-specific, and largely in vitro or rodent models (PMIDs 26317470, 35075293, 27600654). Therefore the evidence base best supports "Existing": a credible but limited human association reported in the literature, without independent replicating primary studies here.

Only two articles in this list address cataract: the Saudi genomic analysis of pediatric cataract identifying novel candidate disease genes (PMID 22935719) and the AOS thesis describing phenotypes of recessive pediatric cataract in children with homozygous gene mutations (PMID 26622071), which appears to draw on largely the same Saudi cohort/candidate gene set rather than an independent replication. This supports at most a single credible human report of a homozygous RNLS variant in a cataract family, i.e., "candidate gene" status, not replicated causation in independent probands, so Established cannot be defended (I cannot cite two independent variant-level studies). All other RNLS literature concerns renalase biology in kidney, cardiac, pancreatic, oncologic and type 1 diabetes contexts (e.g., PMIDs 36196172, 39988068, 38453145), with no mechanistic link to lens biology, so they add nothing to the cataract association. Some residual probability is retained for Hypothesized/Novel in case RNLS is merely listed incidentally among many candidate loci in the Saudi cohort papers.

Most of the strongest evidence linking KCTD13 to neurodevelopmental phenotypes comes from the multigenic 16p11.2 BP4-BP5 CNV (PMIDs 26391891, 25937446, 30518945, 25695269), which cannot isolate KCTD13 from neighbouring dosage-sensitive genes, and from non-human/in vitro models (zebrafish overexpression/knockdown PMID 22596160; mouse knockouts PMIDs 29088697, 30590535, 33436060; iPSC-derived neurons PMID 31402430; organoids PMID 36877372). Direct human variant-level evidence is limited to a single case with a de novo structural alteration disrupting KCTD13 and autism reported within PMID 22596160, and two rare predicted-damaging coding variants each seen in one schizophrenia patient without functional or segregation validation (PMID 27668412). This is credible but not replicated, definitive clinical evidence, so Established is not supportable (no two independent gene-specific proband/family studies). Existing is therefore the best fit, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized because the bulk of causal support is model-organism and cellular biology (RhoA/CUL3, ERBB, purine metabolism; PMIDs 33409479, 38489388).

The strongest direct human genetic evidence is a single publication (PMID 27106596) reporting two multiplex consanguineous families with the same homozygous truncating TNIK variant segregating with autosomal recessive non-syndromic ID, supported by autozygome/linkage and loss of protein. Because this is only one report (with a shared, possibly founder, mutation), the criterion of at least two independent publications with patient variants is not met, so Established cannot be confidently assigned. Supporting evidence comes from hiPSC models of patient-derived TNIK mutations disrupting PSD signaling (PMID 38638602) and from TNIK's synaptic biology and interactions with ID-associated scaffolds CNKSR2/CC2D1A (PMIDs 32235845, 40010432, 40667103), which are functional/mechanistic rather than clinical-genetic. Additional literature links TNIK to schizophrenia and other neuropsychiatric traits (PMIDs 20838393, 31382054, 31813803), reinforcing biological plausibility. Overall this best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" and "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles mention schizophrenia; the AP2A2 literature here concerns Alzheimer's disease pathology and the MUC6 VNTR locus (PMIDs 31748784, 32357373, 34820873), dementia methylation (35299244), hereditary spastic paraplegia (38772452), coronary artery disease (30086706), cancer, and nicotine addiction (29532581). No human genetic study reports variants in AP2A2 associated with schizophrenia or a recognized schizophrenia endophenotype, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small amount of weight goes to Hypothesized because AP2A2 encodes an AP-2 clathrin adaptor subunit central to synaptic vesicle endocytosis and neurotrophin signaling, and the HSP report shows neurodevelopmental/neuronal phenotypes (intellectual disability, altered axon initial segments), biology broadly plausible for psychiatric disease. Nevertheless, these are indirect and not schizophrenia-specific, so the evidence best fits Novel.

The primary human genetic evidence linking CTNNA3 to ARVC rests essentially on a single study (PMID 23136403), which identified αT-catenin variants in ARVC patients; a subsequent independent screening cohort (PMID 21254927) found no disease-causing CTNNA3 mutations, and other candidate-gene screens (PMID 23858024) did not establish causality. Additional human reports involve related but distinct phenotypes (DCM/NDLVC from an intragenic deletion, PMID 42290130; a homozygous splice variant with DCM and arrhythmia, PMID 42471840; rare deletions in atrial fibrillation, PMID 40050430) or list CTNNA3 as background in databases and gene panels (PMID 25676813, 34095246, 25837155). Supportive but non-genetic human/in vitro data show reduced αT-catenin and plakophilin-2 expression in ARVC myocardium and siRNA knockdown effects (PMID 35628349), plus mechanistic reviews of αT-catenin at the area composita (PMID 29746206). Because I cannot cite two independent primary studies reporting single-gene CTNNA3 variants causing ARVC in separate probands/families, "Established" is not warranted; the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful weight on "Hypothesized" given the negative replication and largely mechanistic support.

PMID 21922598 provides primary evidence: linkage/autozygosity mapping in a consanguineous family with febrile seizures and temporal lobe epilepsy identified a homozygous CPA6 missense variant (p.Ala270Val), plus a heterozygous p.Gly267Arg variant in three additional unrelated sporadic TLE patients, with functional validation. PMID 23105115 independently screened further patients with febrile seizures and focal (including temporal lobe) epilepsy, identifying additional deleterious CPA6 variants with reduced extracellular enzyme activity, and PMID 25875328 reported two novel missense mutations in epilepsy patients with functional characterization. A clinical case report of familial temporal lobe epilepsy type 5 (OMIM 614417) attributed to a CPA6 mutation (PMID 32207733) and reviews of FTLE molecular typing (PMID 35111581) further support the gene–disease relationship. Animal/in vitro work (zebrafish knockdown, enzymology) provides supportive mechanistic plausibility but is not needed for the human genetic evidence. Some residual uncertainty remains regarding the strength/penetrance of heterozygous variants, hence a portion of probability assigned to Existing.

The primary evidence is a single positional-cloning study (PMID 22226084) reporting a segregating p.Leu811Val variant in one Chinese autosomal-dominant coloboma family plus a p.Ala57Thr variant in three MAC patients, supported by zebrafish knockdown/rescue. A second, independent human report (PMID 24281366) found an ABCB6 variant in a coloboma/microphthalmia proband, but explicitly with incomplete penetrance and alongside other candidate variants, making it supportive rather than definitive. A review of MAC genetic architecture (PMID 24859618) lists ABCB6 among MAC genes but flags variable confidence levels across genes. Counter-considerations weaken causality: most ABCB6 literature concerns the Lan(-) blood group, dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria, familial pseudohyperkalemia and porphyria (PMIDs 22958180, 24689682, 23519333, 23180570, 34724702), and Lan-null individuals lacking ABCB6 reportedly have no ocular disease. Therefore the association is credible and human-based but limited/not definitively replicated, best fitting "Existing" with some probability of "Established."

Only one human genetic report in the list (PMID 23603806) describes a single consanguineous family/proband with a homozygous MRPL12 missense variant (p.Ala181Val) causing growth retardation, neurological deterioration, multiple respiratory chain deficiency and impaired mitochondrial translation — the phenotype corresponding to combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 45. This is credible, functionally supported evidence but is limited to a single proband, so replication in independent families is lacking, precluding "Established." The remaining literature (MRPL12 in cancers, diabetic kidney disease, AKI, p53/Nrf2 regulation, MIPEP substrate processing, Drosophila mRpL12) supports the gene's biology in mitochondrial transcription and OXPHOS but does not report disease-causing human variants, which would only support "Hypothesized." Accordingly, most weight goes to Existing with a small residual for Established and Hypothesized.

Two independent human studies report single-gene variants segregating with nonsyndromic hearing loss: PMID 24039609 identified a homozygous missense change (c.794T>C; p.Leu265Ser) at the DFNB88 locus in a large consanguineous Pakistani family with recessive nonsyndromic deafness, and PMID 29713870 reported a novel missense variant (c.512A>G; p.His171Arg) co-segregating in a five-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant progressive nonsyndromic hearing loss, with supporting functional assays. These are supported by an Elmod3 knockout mouse showing progressive hearing loss and stereocilia defects (PMID 31628468) and iPSC modeling of the c.512A>G variant (PMID 37708136). The 2p11.2 microdeletion reports (PMIDs 30284680, 31800155, 38137045, 30736458) span multiple genes and therefore only provide supportive, not gene-specific, evidence. Some uncertainty remains because each mode of inheritance rests on a single family with modest replication, so a portion of the probability is retained for "Existing".

Disertori et al. (PMID 23275345) reported the homozygous NPPA p.Arg150Gln variant segregating with autosomal recessive atrial dilated cardiomyopathy with standstill evolution in 13 affected individuals from multiple Italian families, establishing recessive causation in humans. Independent primary reports provide replication in additional probands: PMID 40838933 (the 15th documented case with the homozygous c.449G>A variant), PMID 41590864 (a young homozygous carrier with atrial dilated cardiomyopathy/AF), and PMID 37363091 (a homozygous NPPA variant with fibrotic atrial myopathy, heterozygous parents). Natural-history follow-up (PMID 42015515) and a review (PMID 41464675) further consolidate the genotype–phenotype relationship, while other papers concern AF, hypertension, or mouse models and serve only as supportive biology. The convergence of multiple independent human probands/families with the same recessive mechanism supports the Established category, with a small residual probability that some reports are re-descriptions of overlapping cohorts.

Two articles report human probands with STT3B variants and a CDG phenotype: PMID 23842455 describes a homozygous intronic STT3B mutation (c.1539+20G>T) in a consanguineous family with neurologic abnormalities, hypotonia and hypoglycosylation, with rescue by wild-type cDNA and isoform-specific acceptor glycosylation defects; PMID 32253875 independently reports a novel homozygous STT3B variant (c.38C>G, p.Ser13Trp) in an unrelated child with CDG-Ix features. These are single, unrelated probands rather than large cohorts, and the second report offers little functional validation, so the evidence—while replicated—is thin, keeping substantial weight on "Existing." Supporting mechanistic and in vitro work (PMIDs 29282902, 25460543, 25792706, 31101650) establishes STT3B's essential role in N-glycosylation and CDG biology but is not itself patient-variant evidence. Related MAGT1 (STT3B complex accessory subunit) CDG cases further support pathway relevance.

The primary evidence is the original discovery paper (PMID 24094747), which reported a nonsense AGBL1 mutation segregating in a large late-onset FCD family plus additional unrelated probands with a second missense allele, and showed altered TCF4 interaction — this defines FECD8. Supporting but weak human data come from a targeted NGS study of Han Chinese corneal dystrophy patients reporting a novel AGBL1 variant (PMID 31555324), and screening cohorts (PMIDs 30267097, 42180433) which largely failed to confirm pathogenicity. Importantly, a systematic review (PMID 37441688) and a dedicated reassessment (PMID 40244234) found no AGBL1 expression in corneal endothelium, incomplete segregation, and unaffected carriers, arguing against causality. Most other papers merely restate the association as background (PMIDs 26310151, 34130750, 29799290, 33063975), which is citation rather than independent replication. Therefore the evidence is best described as limited and contested — "Existing" rather than "Established."

Neither article addresses LCAT deficiency or lipid/lipoprotein metabolism. PMID 23105016 links DTHD1 to a novel syndromic retinal dystrophy candidate gene in a consanguineous cohort, and PMID 28034876 mentions DTHD1 only as a downregulated target of miR-3131 in hepatocellular carcinoma. There is no genetic, functional, or pathway-based evidence connecting DTHD1 to lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency, and no biologically relevant mechanism is proposed. The co-mentions are incidental, supporting a "Novel" classification, with a small residual allowance for unassessed biological plausibility.

Primary evidence: PMID 23918663 reports a large consanguineous Pakistani MCPH family with a homozygous CDK6 missense variant c.589G>A p.(Ala197Thr) mapped by homozygosity mapping and confirmed by exome sequencing, with supporting patient-fibroblast centrosomal defects, defining the MCPH12 locus. PMID 40801391 independently identifies a second consanguineous MCPH family with the same homozygous CDK6 variant, refining the MCPH12 critical region and demonstrating a Pakistani founder haplotype. PMID 41856556 further reports CDK4 and CDK6 variants in patients with primary microcephaly with functional cell-cycle/apoptosis consequences. Supporting mechanistic work (PMID 36095192) shows the microcephaly-causing CDK6 mutation disrupts outer radial glia expansion, while reviews (25951892, 30086807, 24780602, 26050940) list CDK6 as the MCPH12 gene as known background rather than new evidence. Some residual uncertainty for "Existing" remains because the two families share a single founder variant, but two independent probands/families in humans support Established.

MAP2K2/MEK2 is definitively linked to cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome (PMIDs 17366577, 19156172, 17704260, 38136934), a RASopathy that clinically overlaps with Noonan syndrome, but direct evidence for MAP2K2 causing classic Noonan syndrome is limited. The strongest human data are a familial MAP2K2 mutation with Noonan-like facies and café au lait spots suggesting neurofibromatosis–Noonan phenotype (PMID 24311457) and one Dutch patient clinically diagnosed with NS carrying a MAP2K2 variant, though later reclassified as CFC (PMID 23885229). Counterevidence exists: no MEK1/MEK2 mutations were found among 75 NS patients (PMID 19156172), and MEK2 variants were seen only in CFC, not NS, in a large cohort (PMID 17704260). Most other listed papers cite MAP2K2 as background in RASopathy panels rather than providing new causal proband-level NS evidence, so replication for NS specifically is not met; "Existing" is the best fit with some probability for Established given the phenotypic continuum.

phenotype: fetal akinesia-cerebral and retinal hemorrhage syndrome
justification: The only article directly reporting the specific phenotype is PMID 23092955, which describes a homozygous DNM2 p.Phe379Val mutation in three consanguineous patients with a lethal congenital syndrome of fetal akinesia, joint contractures, hypotonia, skeletal abnormalities, and brain/retinal hemorrhages, supported by in vitro and zebrafish functional data. This constitutes a single consanguineous family/report rather than multiple independent probands, so replication in independent families is lacking and "Established" cannot be supported. All other papers concern DNM2 in centronuclear myopathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, or severe neonatal congenital myopathy (e.g., PMID 30208955, 36324371, 20127478), which are allelic conditions supporting biological plausibility but not the same phenotype. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (if the described patients are counted as independent probands) and "Hypothesized" (given the heavy reliance on functional/animal data).

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary genetic findings linking ABCB6 missense variants to familial pseudohyperkalemia: PMID 23180570 mapped and sequenced three multigenerational FP families identifying cosegregating codon-375 mutations; PMID 27151991 analyzed three new families with novel mutations (V454A, R276W, R276W/R723Q) and demonstrated increased K+ efflux functionally; PMID 24947683 identified a novel mutation in two unrelated blood donors with FP; and case reports PMID 35372423 (R375W) and PMID 41665094 (R375W) add independent probands. Population/blood-bank studies (PMID 33960432) further link the R723Q allele to accelerated refrigerated potassium leak. Review literature (PMIDs 27756835, 29713289, 37679660, 29051181) consistently cites ABCB6 as the FP causative gene. This constitutes replicated human evidence in independent probands and families, meeting the Established threshold.

phenotype: sacral agenesis-abnormal ossification of the vertebral bodies-persistent notochordal canal syndrome
justification: No article in this set reports its own patient cohort with the specific syndrome (sacral agenesis–abnormal vertebral ossification–persistent notochordal canal); the only mention of TBXT and sacral agenesis appears as background citation in the CDX2 paper (PMID 34671974), which is a citation rather than primary evidence. However, there is credible primary human genetic evidence linking TBXT variants to closely related axial/vertebral phenotypes: a multigenerational family with congenital vertebral malformations segregating T c.596A>G (PMID 37751845), a de novo TBXT missense variant in congenital scoliosis (PMID 32672867), and additional CVM candidate findings (PMIDs 41751889, 38499212). These represent well-recognized overlapping notochord/vertebral developmental phenotypes, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established," since replication for this exact syndrome in independent probands is not demonstrated here. Strong supporting biology (notochord enhancers, tail-loss/Tbxt mouse models, chordoma dependence) provides mechanistic plausibility, justifying meaningful weight on "Hypothesized," while "Novel" is essentially excluded.

Two human reports describe ABCA5-specific lesions in patients with congenital generalized hypertrichosis (OMIM 135400, the hypertrichosis–gingival hyperplasia spectrum): PMID 24831815 identified a homozygous splice-donor variant in intron 32 of ABCA5 with functional follow-up in patient hair follicles, and PMID 35150007 reported the first intragenic ABCA5 deletion in an unrelated autosomal recessive hypertrichosis family — both are gene-specific and independent, supporting Established. However, the supporting evidence in these families is dominated by hypertrichosis, with the gingival fibromatosis component less clearly documented, and PMID 41574449 shows that three CGHGH patients carry multigene 17q24.2-q24.3 rearrangements (ABCA5/ABCA6/ABCA9/ABCA10, MAP2K6, KCNJ2/16) and argues that chromatin/TAD disruption rather than ABCA5 alone may drive the phenotype, which weakens single-gene attribution. Large CNVs (e.g., the 1.3 Mb deletion in PMID 24831815) cannot single out ABCA5. Remaining papers concern Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, lysosomal biology, cardiomyopathy, or drug resistance and are not relevant to this phenotype except as mechanistic (lysosomal/lipid) background.

The primary human genetic evidence comes from a single sibling pair with compound heterozygous KPNA7 exon 7 variants (Pro339Ala, Glu344Gln) presenting with infantile spasms, intractable epilepsy (Lennox-Gastaut-like) and cerebellar malformation (PMID 24045845). A follow-up functional study on the same family's variants showed the E344Q substitution impairs NLS binding and nuclear import in human iPSC-derived neurons (PMID 32179771), which strengthens but does not independently replicate the association, as it involves the same proband family. Other reports (PREMBA, otosclerosis, mouse Kpna7, zebrafish maternal crispants, viral NLS import studies) either address unrelated phenotypes or merely restate the epilepsy link as background, so they do not constitute additional probands. With only one family and no independent replication, the evidence is credible but limited, meeting the criteria for "Existing" rather than "Established."

TSEN54 is unambiguously an established human disease gene, with numerous independent probands and families carrying biallelic variants (e.g., the common p.A307S plus novel missense/splice alleles) causing pontocerebellar hypoplasia types 2, 4 and 5 — a cerebellar degeneration/hypoplasia syndrome (PMIDs 20952379, 21368912, 23307886, 21824568, 32697043, 39634246). However, the specific phenotype queried, cerebellar ataxia, is only variably documented in these patients, who more often show dyskinesia, dystonia and spasticity with profound psychomotor retardation; ataxia was noted in a minority of PCH patients in cohort studies (41825724). The single report of a direct ataxia phenotype (PMID 24938831, familial late-onset ataxia with a novel heterozygous TSEN54 c.254A>T) is of uncertain pathogenicity (monoallelic, single family) and has not been replicated. Zebrafish tsen54 knockdown (21273289) supports the mechanism but is non-human and cannot upgrade the evidence. Thus the strongest reading is credible human evidence linking TSEN54 to a cerebellar degenerative phenotype strongly related to ataxia (Existing), with a substantial but lesser probability that curators would treat the PCH spectrum as Established for cerebellar ataxia.

phenotype: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies
justification: Multiple independent human studies report point (non-CNV) variants in KIF4A in patients with neurodevelopmental phenotypes: Willemsen et al. identified KIF4A variants in X-linked intellectual disability families with synaptic functional support (PMID 24812067); a novel missense variant (p.Leu533Phe) segregated in four affected brothers with polymicrogyria, epilepsy and ID (PMID 39268972); the phenotype was expanded to include hydrocephalus, brain, renal/urogenital, lymphatic, eye and dental anomalies in additional probands (PMID 34346154); an additional pediatric case of XLID100 was reported (PMID 40372222); a fetal anomaly exome study identified a likely causal KIF4A variant (PMID 30679815); and a patient-derived R728Q variant was mechanistically validated in mice showing developmental delay and seizure susceptibility (PMID 36482480). These constitute replicated evidence in independent human probands/families with single-gene variants, precisely matching "complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies." Some remaining uncertainty stems from missense-variant interpretation caveats explicitly noted by the authors and from CNV-based reports (PMIDs 31085274, 33982443, 30298503) that cannot isolate KIF4A, so a small share is left for "Existing."

The only primary human evidence linking DNAH8 to PCD itself is the diagnostic exome study (PMID 24307375), which identified a homozygous truncating DNAH8 variant in a PCD cohort and explicitly labels it a "presumptive new PCD gene" — a single, non-replicated proband, so Established cannot be supported. Subsequent PCD cohort work treats DNAH8 findings as variants of uncertain significance, with normal ciliary ultrastructure in the DNAH8/HYDIN case (PMID 37998386) and VUS status in another report (PMID 40371404), which weakens but does not eliminate the association. Strong replicated human genetic evidence exists instead for DNAH8 in outer-dynein-arm-deficient sperm flagella (MMAF/asthenozoospermia; PMIDs 32619401, 32681648, 33704367, 36308074, 33611675), a motile-axoneme dynein defect that is a recognized component/mechanism of PCD phenotypes, supporting "Existing." Notably, DNAH8 appears sperm-axoneme restricted rather than respiratory-cilia localized (PMID 31178125), and mouse knockouts show flagellar/androgen phenotypes rather than airway ciliopathy, which supports some probability for "Hypothesized" only.

A human GWAS of nonsyndromic metopic craniosynostosis identified a genome-wide significant intronic BMP7 variant (rs6127972) that replicated in an independent non-Hispanic white case-control sample and showed functional plausibility via a differentially methylated enhancer/CTCF site in patient-derived suture mesenchymal stem cells (PMID 32266521). A follow-up targeted sequencing study of the associated 20q13 region in mNCS child-parent trios extends but does not yet establish causality (PMID 35627201). No article reports pathogenic coding variants in BMP7 segregating in multiple independent probands or families, so "Established" is not supported. Supporting biological plausibility comes from Bmp7 expression in developing calvarial sutures and BMP-mediated regulation of suture osteogenesis (PMIDs 10467942, 12710966, 23624389), which would only justify "Hypothesized" alone; combined with the replicated human association, "Existing" is the best fit.

The only primary human genetic evidence linking RGS6 to a neurodevelopmental phenotype is a single consanguineous Tunisian family with autosomal recessive congenital cataract, intellectual disability and microcephaly, in which a homozygous splice-acceptor variant (c.1369-1G>C) was identified (PMID 25525169). A subsequent study (PMID 38332109) provides mechanistic support by showing this variant shifts RGS6 isoform splicing, but it analyzes the same variant rather than a new independent proband, and notes that global Rgs6 knockout mice lack an ID phenotype, weakening causal certainty. Other human data are association-level and for related but distinct traits (schizophrenia enhancer RNA, IQ/educational attainment gene sets via MEF2C targets, alcohol dependence), while much of the remaining literature is mouse/in vitro biology (anxiety/depression, dopaminergic neurodegeneration, hippocampal neurogenesis), supporting only a hypothesized/biologically plausible role. Because I cannot cite two independent probands or families demonstrating causation, Established is not justified; the evidence best fits "Existing."

RPS20 germline truncating variants were first identified by linkage plus exome sequencing in a large Finnish family with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma explicitly LACKING mismatch-repair deficiency (PMID 24941021), i.e., familial colorectal cancer type X rather than true Lynch syndrome; additional independent probands/families have been reported (PMIDs 33193653 Amsterdam-I family, 39920491 de novo frameshift, 32424863, and validation review 27713038). Thus the human genetic evidence links RPS20 to the Amsterdam-criteria/HNPCC spectrum that is clinically the differential diagnosis of Lynch syndrome, but is defined by the absence of MMR-deficiency, so it cannot be called an "Established" cause of Lynch syndrome itself. Furthermore, recent large-scale analyses (PMIDs 40865030, 42274899) explicitly question whether RPS20 is even a proven CRC predisposition gene, weakening the case for replication-level certainty. Functional/in vitro work (PMIDs 35682850, 38290548) supports a plausible mechanism (ribosome biogenesis defects) but is cell-based and only contributes to a hypothesized biological link. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing": credible but limited and contested human data for a Lynch-related (MMR-proficient HNPCC) phenotype.

Three independent human genetic reports describe FBXO32 variants segregating with familial DCM: PMID 26753747 (homozygous FBXO32 variant identified in a family with DCM via exome sequencing), PMID 26768247 (a distinct consanguineous family with a homozygous substitution in FBXO32 causing autosomal recessive DCM, identified by homozygosity mapping plus WES), and PMID 36344977 (a novel likely pathogenic FBXO32 variant in an Iranian DCM family). These are separate probands/families from different populations, satisfying replication. Functional support in patient hearts and cells (PMID 34272480) demonstrates a plausible mechanism through impaired autophagy and CHOP/ATF2-mediated ER-stress apoptosis, strengthening causality. Remaining uncertainty reflects the rarity of reports and the possibility that some cohorts overlap or that classification remains "limited/moderate" by strict curation standards, hence substantial weight also on Existing; other listed papers (muscle atrophy, cancer, UPS expression studies) are supportive biology only.

Direct human genetic evidence for KITLG in Waardenburg syndrome type 2 comes principally from PMID 26522471, which identified a segregating heterozygous missense variant (c.310C>G, p.Leu104Val) in a single small WS2 family, supported by in vitro functional work; this is one family only. A second potential independent report is PMID 28504826 ("Pigmented macules in Waardenburg syndrome type 2 due to KITLG mutation"), but only a title is available and its independence and variant details cannot be verified, so replication is not firmly demonstrable. Other KITLG papers describe related but distinct phenotypes (isolated unilateral/asymmetric hearing loss, biallelic hypomelanosis with SNHL, familial progressive hyper-/hypopigmentation: PMIDs 39918572, 35543077, 21368769), which support pathogenic mechanism and phenotypic overlap but are not WS2F per se. The remaining WS cohort/review articles (PMIDs 38391765, 39338160, 41516007, 41795619) merely list KITLG as a known WS gene without reporting their own KITLG-positive probands, so they count as citations rather than replication. Overall, the relationship is clearly real and human-based but with limited independent proband-level replication, favoring "Existing" with substantial probability for "Established".

The only primary evidence is PMID 26339676, which reports a novel autosomal recessive PRIMA1 mutation causing nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy in a single family — credible but not replicated in independent probands. PMID 38966089 is a review that lists PRIMA1 among sleep-related hypermotor (nocturnal frontal lobe) epilepsy genes, restating the same finding as background rather than providing new evidence, and it explicitly notes that genotype–phenotype correlations remain unclear for most of these genes. Other PRIMA1 papers concern carotid intima-media thickness, depression methylation, borderline personality disorder, restless legs syndrome, goose fatty liver, and pig cortisol, none of which bear on frontal lobe epilepsy causation. Since fewer than two independent human studies demonstrate causal variants, "Established" cannot be supported, and the biology (PRIMA1 anchors acetylcholinesterase, affecting cholinergic transmission, consistent with the nicotinic receptor genes implicated in NFLE) reinforces plausibility of the single-family report.

Two or more independent human studies report bi-allelic APC2 variants in patients with intellectual disability/developmental delay: PMID 25753423 identified a homozygous frameshift in APC2 in siblings with Sotos-like features and intellectual disability, and PMID 31585108 reported 12 individuals from 8 unrelated families with bi-allelic APC2 mutations causing lissencephaly, subcortical heterotopia, and global developmental delay. Additional independent human reports include compound heterozygous missense variants with Sotos features and epilepsy (PMID 33161245) and recessive missense variants in epilepsy cohorts (PMID 37657306/38523034), which reference the established ID/cortical dysplasia phenotype. Supportive functional and mouse data (Apc2−/− mice with impaired learning) reinforce plausibility but are not needed for the human evidence base. Points are concentrated on Established, with a small allowance for the possibility that the specific OMIM entity "MRD/MRT74" is nosologically distinct from the reported APC2 phenotypes.

phenotype: early-childhood-onset neurodegeneration with retinitis pigmentosa, sensorineural hearing loss, and demyelinating peripheral neuropathy
justification: The only primary human genetic evidence here is a single consanguineous family with a homozygous truncating KLC4 variant (c.853_871del19) causing progressive complicated spastic paraplegia (PMID 26423925), plus one proband with a suspected autosomal-dominant HSP variant whose functional testing was done in a humanized C. elegans model (PMIDs 37565267/36789438). No article in this list reports patients with the specific constellation of early-childhood-onset neurodegeneration with retinitis pigmentosa, sensorineural hearing loss and demyelinating peripheral neuropathy, so Established cannot be supported (no two independent probands/families with that phenotype). The complicated, multisystem neurodegenerative HSP phenotype is a plausible overlapping/allelic presentation, which supports "Existing" as the most likely category, though evidence is limited to essentially one family. Supporting mechanistic data from zebrafish klc4 mutants (PMID 36222498) and the worm model bolster biological plausibility (kinesin-1 cargo transport in long axons, sensory neuron arborization), justifying substantial weight on Hypothesized if the phenotype match is judged insufficient.

Multiple independent human studies report causative PRICKLE1 variants in epilepsy patients within their own results: PMID 18976727 identified a homozygous PRICKLE1 mutation in three separate PME-ataxia pedigrees; PMID 21276947 found heterozygous PRICKLE1 mutations in epilepsy patients with functional validation; PMID 20842693 described PRICKLE1 progressive myoclonus epilepsy in Southern Italian families; PMID 30564977 reported compound heterozygous variants in a fatal seizure case; PMID 29790814 and 30345727 report de novo/novel variants with myoclonic epilepsy and epileptic encephalopathy; PMID 31035234 describes an autosomal dominant PME family. GeneReviews entry (PMID 20301774) confirms PRICKLE1-related disorders as a recognized clinical entity. Animal models (mouse, fly) corroborate the mechanism but are not needed to reach the threshold. Evidence is replicated across independent probands and families, satisfying "Established."

Only one article in this set provides primary patient-level genetic evidence: PMID 38569017 identified biallelic loss-of-function TNNI1 variants (p.R14H/c.190-9G>A, homozygous p.R14C) in three families with early-onset progressive weakness and nemaline rods on histology, plus dominant gain-of-function variants (p.R174Q, p.K176del) with rods in one family, supported by zebrafish and myofiber physiology. Although this single report includes multiple independent families, no second independent publication in this list replicates the TNNI1–nemaline myopathy link, so the criterion of at least two evidentiary PMIDs is not met and "Established" cannot be fully endorsed. The other TNNI1 papers concern arthrogryposis (PMID 34934811), sudden infant death thin-filament variants (PMID 30886088), cardiomyocyte maturation markers, oncology, or a different gene (TNNT1, PMID 25430424), and thus do not add nemaline myopathy evidence. Accordingly the weight sits predominantly on "Existing," with residual probability on "Established" given the strength and multi-family nature of the single human study.

Only one primary human genetic study links SPP2 to retinitis pigmentosa (PMID 26459573), reporting a p.Gly97Arg variant in a single Chinese family with autosomal dominant RP, supported by exome sequencing, linkage, in vitro cellular retention data, and zebrafish photoreceptor phenotypes. This is a single family/proband report with no independent replication cohorts in the provided literature, so the "Established" threshold (two or more independent studies with patient variants) is not met. The GeneReviews overview (PMID 20301590) may list SPP2 as background but is not independent evidence. All other papers concern homonymous or unrelated uses of "SPP2" (sphingosine-1-phosphate phosphatase 2, yeast splicing factor Spp2, rat blood pressure/bone QTL, lipid GWAS locus) and do not bear on RP. Hence the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Hypothesized" given the strong functional/animal-model component.

The only primary human genetic evidence is PMID 26339676, which reported a homozygous PRIMA1 mutation causing autosomal recessive nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy in a single family. The other epilepsy-related papers (PMIDs 38966089, 33578443) are reviews or case reports of other genes that merely cite PRIMA1 as a known SHE candidate, which constitutes background citation rather than independent replication. Since no second independent proband/family study is present, the criteria for "Established" are not met. Biological plausibility is supported by PRIMA1's role in anchoring acetylcholinesterase in neuronal membranes and the cholinergic pathway shared with CHRNA4/CHRNB2 SHE genes (PMIDs 12138250, 41096935), but this only reinforces the single human genetic report.

Multiple human genetic association studies report variants in ASPN with OA: the aspartic acid D14 repeat allele originally found in Japanese and replicated in Han Chinese knee OA (PMID 17024313), an ASPN SNP rs13301537 in a Chinese Han knee OA cohort (PMID 25030405), a functional ASPN/CILP polymorphism with hand OA and joint loading (PMID 29233086), and a candidate-gene study implicating ASPN in knee OA (PMID 31665048). However, replication has failed repeatedly in Caucasian populations (PMIDs 16542493, 18434216, 19036616) and two meta-analyses found no overall association of D13/D14/D15 alleles with OA (PMIDs 24306268, 30407347), with high heterogeneity in Asians. Thus the causal link is credible and replicated only within specific East Asian populations and is not definitive, which fits "Existing" better than "Established," though the locus is formally designated OS3 and some reviews treat the ASPN association as among the more compelling ones (PMID 15910695).

The only article whose own results directly link NDUFV2 variants to Leigh syndrome in humans is PMID 26008862, describing two affected siblings (a single family) with complex I deficiency, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and brain atrophy attributed to NDUFV2 mutations. Other primary NDUFV2 human reports describe different, though mechanistically related, complex I phenotypes: early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/encephalopathy (PMID 12754703), progressive cavitating leukoencephalopathy (PMIDs 33811136, 39634239) and optic atrophy (PMID 41234160). PMID 14729820 explicitly contrasts NDUFV2 with NDUFS3, noting NDUFV2 causes cardiomyopathy/encephalomyopathy rather than Leigh syndrome, and reviews (PMIDs 33886098, 42476091) only restate background. Since I cannot cite at least two independent probands/families with NDUFV2-related Leigh syndrome, the evidence supports "Existing" (a credible single report plus a strongly linked complex I deficiency spectrum) rather than "Established".

phenotype: combined pituitary hormone deficiencies, genetic form
justification: The principal primary human evidence is Gaston-Massuet/Casoni-type study (PMID 26764381), which identified two missense variants (p.R92P, p.R400Q) in patients with forebrain and/or pituitary defects and showed reduced repressor activity in vitro and in vivo, alongside conditional mouse models demonstrating a requirement for TCF7L1 in hypothalamo-pituitary axis development. This is a single primary report; the large congenital hypopituitarism cohort (PMID 37165954) may include TCF7L1 but does not clearly present independent probands with TCF7L1 variants in the abstract, and the review (PMID 27974186) merely restates the association as background, which counts as citation, not replication. Therefore the threshold of two independent primary human studies for "Established" is not met. Remaining probability is assigned to "Hypothesized," reflecting the strong developmental/mouse and Wnt-pathway biology (PMIDs 30777146, 31104942, 31987502) that would support a biologically plausible link even absent definitive human genetic proof.

The primary human evidence comes from a single study (PMID 30388401), which identified bi-allelic deleterious mutations in TOP6BL/C11orf80 (along with MEI1 and REC114) in women with recurrent androgenetic complete hydatidiform moles and provided a mechanistic explanation via meiotic DSB failure and maternal chromosome extrusion in Mei1-deficient mouse oocytes. The review (PMID 39322462) restates this as known background rather than providing independent replication, so it counts as citation, not evidence. Other human TOP6BL papers (PMIDs 36732965, 41211863, 41644825) establish biallelic variants causing infertility/azoospermia and oocyte maturation failure — a strongly related meiotic DSB-formation mechanism — reinforcing biological plausibility but not independently replicating the mole phenotype. Remaining papers are mouse, in vitro, or evolutionary/mechanistic studies of the SPO11–TOPOVIBL complex, supporting only a hypothesized-level contribution. Because I cannot cite two independent primary human studies reporting TOP6BL variants in recurrent hydatidiform mole probands, "Existing" is the most appropriate category.

The comprehensive genomic analysis of 142 children with mitochondrial respiratory chain complex deficiencies (PMID 26741492) explicitly nominates PNPLA4 as a novel causative gene, providing direct human genetic evidence linking PNPLA4 variants to mitochondrial disease. However, this is a single cohort study without independent replication, and no other article in the list reports patient-level PNPLA4 variants causing mitochondrial dysfunction. The other papers concern Xp22.31 contiguous copy-number changes (PMIDs 38973237, 29908350, 22314765, 37347056), which span multiple genes (STS, VCX, HDHD1) and cannot isolate PNPLA4, or address lipid metabolism in hepatoma cells and pigs (PMIDs 30918066, 21400235), which are non-human/in vitro and unrelated to mitochondrial phenotypes. Because only one credible human study supports causality, the evidence meets "Existing" but falls short of replicated "Established" status.

Direct human variant-level evidence exists: PMID 35782384 reports four unrelated families with SPTBN5 variants and intellectual disability/developmental delay/autistic features, PMID 40819013 reports a splice variant in two ASD siblings (though co-occurring with a ZCCHC17 nonsense variant, weakening gene attribution), and PMID 41819009 presents an additional case series with systematic review of β-spectrin genes including SPTBN5. This technically approaches replication across independent probands, but the published commentary (PMID 36117916) specifically challenges the original SPTBN5 claim, and SPTBN5 is well known to be tolerant of loss-of-function variation, with older literature (PMID 33847457) explicitly noting no phenotype had been definitively associated with SPTBN5. Other reports implicate SPTBN5 in unrelated phenotypes (oligoasthenoteratozoospermia, ischemic stroke, chicken egg production) or as incidental homozygous variants, providing no NDD support. Given the contested primary evidence and confounded second family, the association is credible but not definitive, favoring "Existing" with substantial weight on "Established."

The primary human evidence is a single consanguineous family with an unclassified oral-facial-digital syndrome carrying a homozygous hypomorphic IFT57 splicing mutation, with functional support showing reduced anterograde ciliary transport and Shh signaling in patient fibroblasts (PMID 27060890); notably, Sanger sequencing of 13 additional OFDS patients was negative. The OFDS review from the same group (PMID 28289185) lists IFT57 among newly identified OFDS genes, but this restates the same cohort/family rather than providing an independent proband. A separate human report describes biallelic IFT57 variants in a Bardet-Biedl syndrome patient (PMID 40273360), confirming IFT57 as a human ciliopathy gene but for a different phenotype. Remaining papers are model organism/in vitro IFT biology (zebrafish ift57 mutants, C. elegans, interactome studies) and support plausibility only. Because only one independent family demonstrates the IFT57–OFD18 link, Established cannot be supported; Existing is the best fit.

The only direct human genetic evidence linking SMARCA1 to psychosis is the exploratory whole-genome sequencing study of multiplex families (PMID 27001614), where a novel private missense variant on the X chromosome segregated with illness in four affected siblings (carried also by an unaffected mother), which is a single family and thus limited, non-replicated evidence supporting "Existing" rather than "Established." Other SMARCA1 papers describe X-linked intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental disorders (PMIDs 41213919, 40316778, 26539891, 18302774) or a multigene deletion in Lowe syndrome (PMID 31376231), which do not single out schizophrenia. Supporting but indirect biology comes from SWI/SNF/chromatin-remodeling involvement in schizophrenia, though those genetic associations concern SMARCA2, a different gene (PMIDs 19363039, 20457675, 28824374). Therefore evidence is best classified as limited human association (Existing), with a substantial residual probability that reviewers would consider it merely biologically plausible (Hypothesized).

Two human reports present primary variant data in independent probands: the original single-patient SEMA3E mutation report in CHARGE syndrome (PMID 15235037) and a novel heterozygous missense variant (p.Ala443Thr) in a fetus with CHARGE syndrome (PMID 31691538). However, both are isolated case reports of missense changes with limited functional/segregation proof, and multiple sources treat SEMA3E as a rare, secondary cause invoked mainly as background while CHD7 explains >90% of cases (PMIDs 33184947, 33844462). Contradictory human data also exist: twins carrying a de novo "CHARGE-associated" SEMA3E variant lacked CHARGE features (PMID 32441320), and a recent report explicitly states the SEMA3E–CHARGE association has been questioned (PMID 41243476). Supporting biology is largely non-human (zebrafish sema3E knockdown recapitulating CHARGE-like craniofacial/neural crest defects, PMID 31464029), which supports Hypothesized rather than Established. Given credible but non-definitive, partially disputed human genetic evidence with fewer than two robust replications, "Existing" is the best fit.

Two human genetic studies report CDK16 variants in patients: the X-exome sequencing of 405 XLID families identified CDK16 as a candidate XLID gene with "potentially deleterious" variants (PMID 25644381), and a systematic chrX analysis reported damaging CDK16 variants in patients with intellectual disability/autism (PMID 36323681). Functional support exists, since patient-derived PCTAIRE-1/CDK16 variants fail to bind cyclin Y and are catalytically inactive (PMID 26205494), and CDK16 substrates (AAK1, dynamin 1, synaptojanin 1) regulate synaptic vesicle trafficking and neurite outgrowth (PMIDs 30880224, 12154078, 16461345). However, the primary genetic reports frame CDK16 as a candidate rather than a definitively validated disease gene, and independent replication in multiple well-characterized probands/families is limited, so the evidence falls short of Established. The remaining articles are cancer, cell-cycle, or developmental biology studies that only co-mention CDK16 without ID-relevant patient variants.

Two independent studies report their own patient-derived genetic evidence: PMID 27023905 mapped DFNB60 in a large consanguineous Tunisian family and identified homozygous SLC22A4 p.Cys113Tyr cosegregating with ARNSHL, plus a second Tunisian consanguineous proband, with functional data showing impaired trafficking and ergothioneine uptake and strial endothelial expression; PMID 33643381 provides an independent replication in a consanguineous Moroccan family with linkage (LOD>3) and the same homozygous p.C113Y variant in six affected individuals. Together these constitute replication in independent families/probands in humans, supporting Established. Counterweights that keep some probability on Existing are the reliance on a single recurrent founder allele in one geographic population, the small number of families, and documented incomplete penetrance (one homozygous normal-hearing sibling), plus no additional variants found in seven other screened deaf patients. Supporting biology (ergothioneine transport, cochlear/OCTN1 expression, otoprotection in animal models: PMIDs 38770822, 38608332) reinforces plausibility but is not itself human genetic evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report causal SLC14A1 (JK) variants identified in their own probands/families: PMID 38275395 found novel null alleles (Gly40Asp, Gly242Glu) and a 5-kb exon 9–10 deletion in donors with serology–genotype discrepancies; PMID 16483143 described a novel splice-site mutation causing Jk-null in a Chinese family; PMID 26969102 identified novel silent JK alleles in Chinese Jk(a–b–) individuals; PMID 27834480 reported a novel JK*B c.1038delG allele in a woman with anti-Jkb; PMID 41965235 described a novel JK*01 c.299C>T allele abolishing Jka expression in two African American donors; PMID 37165957 characterized two new silencing alleles by long-read sequencing. The antithetical Jka/Jkb antigens are directly determined by the c.838G>A (Asp280Asn) SNV in SLC14A1, with complete genotype–phenotype concordance demonstrated in genotyping studies (PMIDs 9734652, 9885013). This is a canonical, replicated human gene–blood group relationship, so Established is overwhelmingly favored.

None of the provided articles address Tourette syndrome at all; the papers concern type 1 diabetes/intestinal barrier in mice (PMID 38493812), ALS models (PMID 41667820), and a systematic review of PTSD GWAS in which FAM120A was among replicated loci (PMID 40195096). PTSD is not a recognized precursor, subtype, or mechanism of Tourette syndrome, so this does not support "Existing." The ALS work is neuronal and in mouse/cell models, giving only a faint, indirect neurobiological rationale that could marginally support "Hypothesized," but there is no tic-disorder-specific expression, pathway, or model evidence. No human genetic study links FAM120A variants to Tourette syndrome, so the relationship is best described as Novel.

No article in this list reports pathogenic or associated SNAI1 variants identified in patients with congenital heart disease; there are no probands or families with SNAI1 genotypes, so Established is excluded and Existing is poorly supported. Instead, the evidence is strongly mechanistic: SNAI1/Snail1 is a core driver of endocardial and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition underlying endocardial cushion, septal, and valve formation (PMIDs 42600378, 20890042, 32226439), and Snai1 is downstream of the Sin3A/Sap130 complex implicated in the Ohia mouse model of hypoplastic left heart syndrome (PMID 36975863). Human in vitro work on discrete subaortic stenosis shows shear-stress-induced SNAI1 upregulation in endocardial endothelial cells (PMID 41606256), and animal/stem-cell models link Snail1/Snai2 dysregulation to CHD-like phenotypes (PMIDs 31211496, 32276728, 41460181, 30038385). Several other listed papers concern cancer, kidney fibrosis, or FTD/ALS genetics and are not relevant to CHD causation. This pattern fits Hypothesized: strong biological and animal-model plausibility without human variant evidence.

phenotype: pontocerebellar hypoplasia, hypotonia, and respiratory insufficiency syndrome, neonatal lethal
justification: All human patient evidence for the neonatal lethal pontocerebellar hypoplasia/hypotonia/respiratory insufficiency phenotype points to ATAD3A as the driver gene; ATAD3C appears only because it lies within, or provides the NAHR substrate for, multi-gene structural rearrangements at the ATAD3 locus (PMIDs 28549128, 27640307, 32004445, 33575671, 36061954). Such deletions/duplications spanning ATAD3C, ATAD3B and ATAD3A cannot attribute causality to ATAD3C specifically, so Established is effectively excluded; no article reports an intragenic, ATAD3C-specific pathogenic variant in independent probands. Some human relevance persists because ATAD3C sequences are incorporated into the disease-causing chimeric fusion alleles (ATAD3B/ATAD3A, ATAD3A/ATAD3C) found in affected patients, supporting an "Existing" but non-definitive association. Functional work showing that ATAD3C is expressed in human cells and acts as a dominant-negative regulator of ATAD3A assembly and OXPHOS (PMID 38092275) provides a strong biological rationale, supporting "Hypothesized." The MYO1H/HSP paper (PMID 35704118) explicitly excluded the ATAD3C variant and concerns a different phenotype.

Only a single human report (PMID 33922911) describes compound heterozygous KIF17 variants (p.Arg419Trp; p.Arg852Cys) co-segregating with microphthalmia and coloboma in two siblings from one Sicilian family; there is no independent replication in other probands or families, so "Established" cannot be supported. The remaining literature is animal/in vitro work showing KIF17 (osm-3/kif17) roles in photoreceptor outer segment development and ciliary transport in zebrafish and mouse (PMIDs 28341548, 20409820, 16782012, 28444310), which provides strong biological plausibility for eye development but not human genetic evidence. Other papers concern neuronal NMDA receptor transport, epilepsy, schizophrenia, and speech disorders, which are unrelated phenotypes. Hence "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability on "Hypothesized" given that the human evidence rests on one small family with in-silico-predicted deleterious missense variants.

phenotype: autosomal dominant combined immunodeficiency due to ERBIN deficiency
justification: The primary human genetic evidence comes from Lyons et al. (PMID 28126831), which described a loss-of-function ERBB2IP (ERBIN) mutation in patients with a connective tissue/atopy phenotype and dysregulated TGF-β–STAT3 signaling, plus a follow-up therapeutic case report in a patient with ERBIN deficiency (PMID 35093604), which likely concerns the same kindred rather than an independent proband. Reviews (PMIDs 37369151, 30466772, 40114756, 37702167) repeatedly list ERBB2IP among hyper-IgE/primary atopic disorder genes, but these restate the association as background rather than provide new probands, so they do not constitute replication. The remaining literature (Erbin in sepsis, colitis, Nod2 signaling, epithelial polarity, cancer) is mechanistic or animal/in vitro and supports only biological plausibility. Because I cannot cite at least two independent human studies with distinct probands demonstrating causality, the evidence best fits "Existing," with some residual probability for "Established" given the disorder is named for the gene.

Most TNNT1 literature concerns the autosomal recessive (Amish and non-Amish) nemaline myopathy, which is not the dominant phenotype in question.
