However, two independent human reports specifically document monoallelic/dominant TNNT1 disease: PMID 29178646 describes a novel autosomal dominant TNNT1 mutation segregating in a large historically documented family with nemaline myopathy, and PMID 35510366 reports a mother–son pair with a heterozygous p.(Asp65Ala) variant (de novo in the mother) with supporting muscle pathology and TPM3-binding functional data. These constitute two independent probands/families with variant-level evidence in humans, supporting an Established classification, though the second paper hedges ("likely caused") and the total number of dominant families remains small, leaving substantial weight on Existing. Remaining recessive case reports and in vitro/zebrafish functional work (e.g., PMIDs 27429059, 15665378) support the gene's biology but not the dominant phenotype directly.

Only one primary human genetic study reports a homozygous TRIM36 missense variant (c.1522C>A, p.Pro508Thr) causing autosomal recessive anencephaly in a single Indian family (PMID 28087737), supported by in vitro functional work showing protein destabilization and microtubule/spindle disruption. The review (PMID 35053362) and the NUAK2 case report (PMID 41008661) merely restate this single family as background, which constitutes citation rather than independent replication. Other articles concern TRIM36 structure, cloning, microtubule binding, or methylation in lead-exposed workers and provide no additional patient-variant evidence. With only one proband/family and no independent replication, the criteria for Established are not met, so Existing is the best fit, with residual probability on Hypothesized given the strong supporting developmental biology.

Only a single article (PMID 28150392) provides direct human genetic evidence: a homozygous loss-of-function KIF15 variant in one consanguineous Saudi family with congenital thrombocytopenia and Pierre-Robin sequence, described as a Braddock-Carey syndrome genocopy (now designated Braddock-Carey syndrome 2). This is a credible, disease-specific report but comes from a single family/proband, with no independent replication in the provided literature. Other papers concern KIF15 in cancers, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis susceptibility, kinesin biology, and mouse/zebrafish mood or axonal phenotypes, which are biologically supportive of a kinesin developmental role but not evidence for this syndrome. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with limited probability given to "Established" pending additional independent families.

The strongest human genetic data link DTNA to left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy rather than to dilated cardiomyopathy per se: a DTNA missense variant segregating in a family with non-isolated LVNC (PMID 16427346), and reviews restating this association as background (PMIDs 19057090, 17729299, 30980206). LVNC frequently manifests with ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction, so it qualifies as a closely related subtype/precursor phenotype supporting "Existing." Direct DCM evidence, however, comes chiefly from a transgenic mouse overexpressing DTNA p.N49S that developed trabeculation, LV dilation and systolic dysfunction (PMID 29118297) — animal, not human — and from regulatory-variant enrichment in DTNA within a mixed pediatric cardiomyopathy WGS cohort (PMID 35288587), which is suggestive but not variant-level proof in DCM probands. Other citations involve HCM (PMID 38551768), sudden unexplained death (PMID 33895855), atrial fibrillation (PMID 35148685), skeletal muscular dystrophy (PMID 36799992), or unrelated phenotypes, and multigene CNVs cannot isolate DTNA. I cannot cite two independent human studies reporting DTNA variants causing DCM in distinct probands/families, so Established is unlikely.

phenotype: inflammatory bowel disease (infantile ulcerative colitis) 31, autosomal recessive
justification: A single credible human report (PMID 33674380) describes a 4-month-old male from a consanguineous family with a homozygous loss-of-function IL37 mutation presenting with infantile IBD, supported by patient-cell and iPSC-derived macrophage functional work showing hyperinflammatory cytokine production. This is one proband only; no second independent family or proband is reported in this list, so replication required for "Established" is absent. Additional supportive but non-causal human data include IL-37 epithelial overexpression in IBD mucosa (PMID 23600829), a case study of a patient with a potential IL37 loss-of-function variant (PMID 36476991), and IL37 variant associations with other inflammatory phenotypes (periodontitis, gout, CAD, SLE, AML), which reinforce biological plausibility. Broader reviews on IL-1 family cytokines in gut homeostasis (PMID 23847622) support a mechanistic role. Therefore "Existing" is most appropriate, with residual probability for "Established" and "Hypothesized".

The primary human genetic evidence comes from PMID 30157172, which reported a homozygous CLCC1 missense variant (c.75C>A, p.D25E) segregating in eight consanguineous Pakistani arRP families with supporting functional work in cells, zebrafish and mice. PMID 35391798 genotyped nine families carrying the same variant, but haplotype analysis shows a single ancient founder mutation, so these are not truly independent alleles/lineages, and the authors note this remains the only CLCC1 RP mutation reported. PMID 38621504 provides mechanistic follow-up on the same p.Asp25Glu variant (interactome, SigmaR1/MAM), which reinforces plausibility but is not independent clinical replication. Other papers link CLCC1 to ALS, neurodegeneration, cholestasis, dystonia or calcium signaling and do not add RP-specific genetic evidence. Thus the association is credible and functionally supported but rests on one founder variant, sitting between Existing and Established.

MYL3 is a well-established hypertrophic/restrictive cardiomyopathy gene (PMIDs 23594557, 33288880, 35288424, 24111713), but none of these implicate arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. The single dedicated candidate-gene study of MYL3 in ARVC/D explicitly found no disease-causing mutations in 14 Spanish ARVC probands (PMID 22421524), i.e., negative evidence. PMID 29709087 examined rare sarcomeric variants in ARVC probands, raising the possibility of phenotypic overlap, but the abstract does not attribute variants to MYL3 specifically; similarly, in the Indian panel study (PMID 38551768) the ARVC cases carried desmosomal, not MYL3, variants. Remaining mentions are incidental co-listings of MYL3 among cardiomyopathy panel genes. Thus no credible human evidence of a causal MYL3–ARVC link exists, with only a weak conceptual sarcomere-overlap rationale supporting a hypothesized relationship.

phenotype: visual impairment and progressive phthisis bulbi
justification: Only one primary human study (PMID 29771303) reports a homozygous missense variant (p.Arg570Gly) in MARK3 segregating in a single consanguineous Pakistani family with congenital vision loss and progressive eye degeneration, supported by Drosophila par-1 knockdown/mutant functional work. This is a single family without independent replication in other probands, so the criterion for "Established" (two or more independent human reports) is not met. A subsequent review (PMID 36581219) restates MARK3's role in ocular/developmental phenotypes as background rather than providing new evidence. The remaining articles concern MARK3 kinase biology, cancer, bone mass, tau phosphorylation, and COVID-19 proteomics, and are not relevant to this phenotype. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with limited probability for Established.

Two human reports provide variant-level evidence: PMID 29581481 identified a homozygous PDHA2 missense variant (p.Met227Val) segregating with azoospermia/sperm immotility in a consanguineous family, though the authors themselves call PDHA2 only a "novel candidate" and the variant is linked in cis-region with a BMPR1B variant, confounding attribution; PMID 35172124 reported a highly deleterious homozygous/hemizygous PDHA2 defect in an individual with non-obstructive azoospermia among a WES cohort. This constitutes limited, not fully definitive, replication in independent probands, so Existing is the most defensible category, with a meaningful chance of Established. Strong supporting biology comes from non-human work: Pdha2 knockout mice are infertile with meiotic recombination and DSB-repair defects (PMIDs 39973374, 40679056), and testis-specific expression/regulation studies (PMIDs 2249846, 20005141, 8024696) — these support Hypothesized but cannot themselves upgrade the human evidence. Novel is essentially excluded given the direct germ-cell biology and human variant reports.

Two independent human genetic studies report biallelic/homozygous CEP112 variants in infertile men: PMID 31654588 identified a nonsense variant (p.Arg166X) in one proband and compound heterozygous missense variants in a second unrelated proband with acephalic spermatozoa, with expression/plasmid evidence of loss of function; PMID 39349455 identified CEP112 mutations in oligoasthenoteratozoospermic patients, supported by a Cep112-deficient mouse recapitulating the phenotype and functional demonstration that patient variants disrupt phase separation and translation. These represent independent probands from separate laboratories, supporting an Established relationship with SPGF44, though the reported phenotypes differ somewhat (acephalic spermatozoa vs. asthenoteratozoospermia) and the total number of families remains small, leaving substantial weight on Existing. The review (PMID 33452591) and the NOA screening study (PMID 40376536) provide contextual rather than primary replicative evidence.

The core evidence is a single human genetics paper (PMID 29478781) reporting two unrelated individuals with distinct homozygous missense variants (p.Pro82Leu, p.Val106Gly) in ATP5F1D, with fibroblast studies showing impaired F1FO ATP synthase assembly, reduced complex V activity, abnormal cristae, and Drosophila rescue/modeling supporting pathogenicity — a compelling case for a Mendelian mitochondrial disorder. However, this is one publication rather than replicated independent reports across multiple studies, so per the stated criteria the evidence does not reach "Established" and should be scored primarily as "Existing." Supporting biological plausibility comes from non-human/in vitro work on the central stalk subunits γ and δ in ATP synthase assembly (PMID 29499186) and from cell-based studies where ATP5F1D loss causes mitochondrial dysfunction (PMID 40817715), plus transcriptomic downregulation in sALS spinal cord (PMID 41009796). Several other listed papers mention Atp5d only incidentally in animal/expression contexts (PMIDs 32096418, 32236796, 34755111, 29312001, 35690344, 24615392, 36686378) and add little disease-variant evidence.

Only a single human genetic report directly links PLCB3 to spondylometaphyseal dysplasia: PMID 29122926 describes a homozygous PLCB3 variant causing a new form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with corneal dystrophy, apparently in one family/cohort, with no independent replicating proband reported in this list. That satisfies "at least one credible human study" but falls short of the two-independent-proband requirement for Established. Supporting biological plausibility comes from the zebrafish plcb3 (schmerle) mutant, which shows Endothelin1-dependent craniofacial skeletal patterning defects requiring Plcβ3 in neural crest cells (PMID 17239364), and from general PLCβ3 signaling studies, but these are animal/in vitro and only bolster the Hypothesized tier. All other listed papers concern unrelated phenotypes (atopic dermatitis, cystic fibrosis inflammation, blood pressure, lipids, COPD, Parkinson's) or enzymology and do not address skeletal dysplasia.

Only one article in this set provides direct human genetic evidence: PMID 29122926 reports a homozygous PLCB3 variant causing a new form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with corneal dystrophy, apparently in a single family/cohort with supporting functional work on phosphoinositide signalling. Since no second, independent report of probands or families with PLCB3 variants and this skeletal-corneal phenotype is present, the criteria for "Established" (at least two independent human genetic reports) are not met. Supporting biology exists: zebrafish plcb3 mutants show craniofacial/skeletal patterning defects downstream of Endothelin1 (PMID 17239364), and other studies characterize PLCβ3 catalytic regulation, reinforcing plausibility but not adding independent human evidence. The remaining papers concern unrelated phenotypes (atopic dermatitis, cystic fibrosis inflammation, blood pressure, lipids, COPD, Parkinson's) and do not bear on this phenotype.

The strongest human evidence is PMID 30377171, which reports a single patient with CHD and heterotaxy carrying a de novo WDR5 mutation, followed by Xenopus functional work showing left–right patterning and ciliogenesis defects — one proband plus model-organism support. PMID 36408368 describes 11 individuals with de novo WDR5 missense variants defining a neurodevelopmental disorder, with heart anomalies noted in only 2 individuals as a minor feature, providing supportive but not definitive cardiac evidence. PMID 33281884 implicates WDR5 only within a multigene CNV in patent ductus arteriosus and cannot single out the gene, so it does not count toward causal replication. Additional papers (e.g., 28669924, 24705355) place WDR5 in COMPASS/KMT2D complexes whose disruption causes CHD-associated syndromes, which is mechanistic/background rather than direct variant evidence. Overall this supports "Existing" — at least one credible human report plus plausible supporting biology — with limited weight for "Established" given the lack of independent replicated CHD probands.

phenotype: indifference to pain, congenital, autosomal dominant
justification: The primary human evidence is PMID 29253101, which identified a novel ZFHX2 point mutation (p.R1913K) segregating with pain insensitivity in six affected individuals across three generations of a single family, supported by BAC transgenic and knockout mouse models showing pain deficits. A second report (PMID 35768377) describes an apparently independent Chinese proband and her mother with a positive ZFHX2 variant and a Marsili-syndrome phenotype, but it is a brief case report with limited variant-level detail and its own review notes only one family reported worldwide, so replication is weak. The remaining articles are non-causal: a mouse behavioral study (PMID 23300874) and a transcriptomic network study of chemotherapy-induced neuropathy (PMID 37623249) provide only supportive biology, and the GeneReviews overview (PMID 29419974) restates the association as background. Overall the gene–disease relationship rests essentially on one well-characterized family plus a single supportive case report, which fits "Existing" (limited evidence) more than robust, replicated "Established" status.

No article in this set links STXBP3 variants to arthrogryposis or fetal akinesia/congenital contractures. The only human genetic evidence (PMIDs 33891011, 40575033) associates STXBP3 variants with very early onset inflammatory bowel disease, sensorineural hearing loss and immune dysregulation — phenotypes unrelated to arthrogryposis. The remaining papers concern Munc18-3/Munc18c biology in GLUT4 trafficking, amylase exocytosis and platelet vesicle transport, none of which involve neuromuscular function or joint contractures. The C. elegans unc-18 rescue study (PMID 8824310) shows paralysis/cholinergic defects rescued by neuronal Munc18-1, while Munc18-3 (STXBP3) explicitly failed to rescue, arguing against a neuromuscular akinesia mechanism for this gene. Only a small residual probability is given to "Hypothesized" because SNARE-mediated cholinergic/neurotransmission biology is loosely relevant to fetal akinesia phenotypes.

Direct human genetic evidence with variants in probands comes from PMID 35917186 (Chen et al.), which reports 46 likely gene-disruptive GIGYF1 variants, including a recurrent frameshift, across two large ASD cohorts with inheritance and phenotype analysis, and from PMID 41646820, an independent de novo variant analysis of 41,367 trios in which GIGYF1 reached exome-wide significance for autism. Supporting human evidence includes PMID 37231097, where rare coding GIGYF1 variants had large effects on adult cognitive function with partial overlap with neurodevelopmental disorder architecture. Animal and mechanistic work (Gigyf1 conditional knockout mice, zebrafish, IGF-1R recycling; PMIDs 36924980, 36189799) supports biological plausibility but counts only toward Hypothesized. Because the strongest single dataset (Chen et al.) partly re-analyzes previously published ASD cohorts, some uncertainty remains as to whether the replication is fully independent, so points are split between Established and Existing. Remaining papers concern metabolic/anthropometric traits (T2D, obesity, grip strength) and are not NDD evidence.

Only one human study (PMID 25957586) reports a homozygous truncating ARL6IP6 variant identified by autozygosity mapping and trio WES in a single consanguineous Saudi family with syndromic CMTC; the authors themselves label it a "novel candidate gene." No independent replication in additional probands or families is present in this list, so the criterion for Established (two or more independent human reports with variants) is not met. The GWAS of early-onset ischemic stroke (PMID 22384361) supports a vascular-related human association with ARL6IP6, consistent with a shared mechanism, adding indirect support. The mucopolysaccharidosis transcriptomic papers (PMIDs 39769211, 38534785) and the mouse febrile seizure QTL paper (PMID 27690330) are unrelated to CMTC and contribute no evidence.

Only one human clinical report (PMID 31039582) identifies a homozygous MRPS25 variant (p.P72L) in a single proband with encephalomyopathy and mitochondrial translation defect, supported by strong functional evidence including rescue by wild-type MRPS25 expression. This is credible, mechanistically compelling evidence but derives from a single family, so replication in independent probands is lacking, precluding "Established". The other two articles (PMID 32376682, 32987154) concern mouse Mrp gene knockouts and expression profiling and do not report human MRPS25 variants, providing only supportive biological plausibility. Consequently, the evidence best fits the "Existing" category.

Three independent human clinical reports present their own patient-level variant data in HS6ST2: PMID 30471091 (two Italian male twins with XLID and severe myopia carrying maternally inherited c.916G>C/G306R, with an in vitro sulfotransferase assay showing reduced activity), PMID 36993824 (a third, unrelated proband with a novel c.979C>T variant and MRXSPM phenotype), and PMID 40686562 (a fourth, unrelated Chinese proband with novel c.764C>A and functional evidence of altered protein expression). These are single-gene point mutations in independent probands, not multigene CNVs, satisfying replication requirements. Supporting mechanistic data come from the Hs6st2 knockout mouse showing memory deficits and impaired hippocampal dendritic spines (PMID 38015989) and X-chromosome association with neuroticism implicating HS6ST2 (PMID 30842574). Some residual uncertainty remains because several variants are formally classified as of uncertain significance and case numbers are very small, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing."

Two independent human family-based reports provide variant-level evidence: PMID 31320686 identified a novel X-linked segregating missense variant (p.Gly161Arg) in CLDN2 in a multiplex family with obstructive azoospermia/epididymal obstruction, and PMID 32149733 described a family in which males carrying a rare CLDN2 missense variant had marked hypercalciuria and kidney stone disease, plus common CLDN2 variants associated with stone risk in two population cohorts. Together these cover the two components of the composite phenotype (obstructive azoospermia with nephrolithiasis), but each family demonstrates only one component, and a targeted screen found CLDN2 mutations are not a common cause of pediatric idiopathic hypercalciuria (PMID 35615069), tempering the strength of replication. Supporting biology comes from claudin-2 knockout mice with hypercalciuria and medullary nephrocalcinosis/Randall's-plaque-like deposits (PMIDs 32149733, 41066193) and altered epididymal claudin expression/blood-epididymis barrier disruption in obstructive azoospermia (PMID 20505168), consistent with the proposed tight-junction mechanism. Many remaining papers concern CLDN2 in IBD, pancreatitis, or cancer and are not relevant to this phenotype. Overall the evidence is credible and gene-specific but only borderline replicated for the full syndrome, so probability is split between Established and Existing.

Only one human genetic study in the list (PMID 31273342) reports ABCC1 as linked to autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss, based on stepwise genetic analysis of a single family (HN-SD01); no second independent proband/family study is present, so the "Established" threshold of replicated human evidence is not met. Supporting biological evidence comes from a mouse Abcc1 knockout model showing cochlear stria vascularis endothelial expression and increased susceptibility to noise-induced hearing loss (PMID 38870779), which is animal data and thus reinforces plausibility rather than human causality. All other articles concern ABCC1/MRP1 in drug efflux, multidrug resistance, chemotherapy toxicity, and transporter pharmacogenomics, and are irrelevant to hearing loss. Therefore a credible but single, non-replicated human report plus strong supportive functional/animal data best fits "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the single family report is considered insufficient.

Only a single human report (PMID 31729093) describes a novel damaging NOTCH3 variant segregating in one family with pediatric inherited thrombocytopenia; this is a single proband/family without independent replication, so it supports "Existing" but not "Established". All other NOTCH3 literature here concerns CADASIL/cerebral small vessel disease, arthritis, fibrosis, and vascular biology, none of which involve platelet counts. Biological plausibility for a hematopoietic role comes from mouse work showing CADASIL-related NOTCH3 mutations drive clonal hematopoiesis and alter HSPC fitness (PMID 39537978), but that is murine and would only support "Hypothesized". Because no second independent human family or proband with NOTCH3-related thrombocytopenia is present, the evidence remains limited and non-definitive.

Only one article in this set presents primary human genetic evidence: PMID 30489636, reporting an XRCC2 mutation causing premature ovarian insufficiency (and non-obstructive azoospermia), which corresponds to the POF17 designation. The remaining supportive citations (PMIDs 34794894, 39359934, 33977503, 32048394) are reviews or papers on other genes that merely restate XRCC2/FANCU as a known POI gene, so they constitute citation rather than independent replication. Because I cannot name at least two primary studies with independent probands/families, "Established" cannot be selected, and the evidence best fits "Existing." The remaining articles concern XRCC2's role in homologous recombination, BCDX2 complex structure, and cancer risk, which provide mechanistic plausibility (meiotic DNA repair defects causing follicle depletion) but not direct POI genetic evidence.

Two independent human reports provide primary genetic evidence: PMID 30358850 describes a homozygous MRPS14 (uS14m) variant in a patient with perinatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis and complex IV deficiency, with functional rescue by wild-type cDNA; PMID 40317698 reports a second, unrelated proband with novel compound heterozygous MRPS14 variants causing Leigh syndrome, supported by reduced MRPS14 and COX2 protein levels. These are two distinct probands with single-gene (not CNV) variants plus supportive functional data, satisfying the criteria for replication, although the total number of reported cases remains very small, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing". PMID 32987154 is expression/biology background across mitoribosomal protein genes and only supports mechanistic plausibility, not causation. No homonym/acronym confusion is present in these articles.

phenotype: global developmental delay with or without impaired intellectual development
justification: Multiple independent primary human genetic studies report biallelic EMC10 variants in patients with global developmental delay/intellectual disability: PMID 32869858 (Saudi family with homozygous splice-acceptor variant c.679-1G>A segregating in two affected siblings), PMID 33531666 (13 individuals from seven families with a recurrent homozygous frameshift variant), PMID 35684946 (10 affected individuals from six independent families with five new biallelic loss-of-function variants), and PMID 35124540 (phenotype of homozygous c.287delG). Additional case reports (PMID 40150819, 40741735, 42362276) expand the phenotype with novel single-nucleotide variants, and the disorder is formally recognized as EMC10-related neurodevelopmental disorder/NEDDFAS (OMIM #619264, GeneReviews PMID 37319253). These are point/frameshift/splice variants, not multigene CNVs, and are replicated across unrelated families and populations. Supporting functional data (expression reduction, Xenopus neural crest, mouse Emc10 models) reinforce the mechanism.

phenotype: male infertility with azoospermia or oligozoospermia due to single gene mutation
justification: None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in RIOK2 in men with azoospermia or oligozoospermia; there are no clinical cohorts, probands, or families described, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The literature instead centers on RIOK2 as an atypical kinase in ribosome biogenesis (PMIDs 23104056, 31390939), cancer biology (23459592, 36518977, 29712692, 38117512), and parasite/plant biology. The only tangential reproductive link is invertebrate: Sj-riok-2 involvement in reproductive processes and egg production in Schistosoma japonicum (29233188) and egg hatching in Strongyloides (32592810), plus developmental expression in parasitic nematodes (28821723) — these are non-mammalian and provide only a weak biological rationale for a role in gametogenesis, supporting a modest Hypothesized weight. Overall the evidence base indicates a Novel gene–phenotype relationship, with some residual probability for Hypothesized based on conserved roles in germ-cell/ribosome-dependent proliferation.

The only primary human genetic evidence is a single whole-exome sequencing study reporting a homozygous GPR161 mutation in one family with pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (PMID 25322266); no independent second proband or family is reported in this list, so replication criteria for "Established" are not met. Review articles (PMID 27974186) merely restate GPR161 among genes implicated in pituitary developmental disorders, which is citation rather than new evidence, and one analysis explicitly annotates the GPR161–PSIS link as "not confirmed" (PMID 28063110). Remaining literature concerns GPR161 biology in Hedgehog/ciliary signaling, neural tube defects, and medulloblastoma predisposition (PMIDs 30256984, 34346313, 38326651), which supports plausible developmental mechanism but not PSIS causation. Thus the evidence best fits "Existing," with a modest residual probability for "Established" and some weight for "Hypothesized" if the single family report is deemed insufficient.

phenotype: triokinase and FMN cyclase deficiency syndrome
justification: Direct human evidence of causation comes from PMID 32004446, which reports bi-allelic TKFC variants in two unrelated families with cataracts and multisystem disease (the eponymous triokinase/FMN cyclase deficiency), supported by functional yeast assays. Independent replication is provided by PMID 38697782 (homozygous TKFC variant abolishing triokinase activity in a patient with isolated immunodeficiency), PMID 39251934 (Egyptian patients with biallelic TKFC variants and expanded phenotype), and PMID 32790068 (TKFC mutations in autosomal recessive hypotrichosis with loose anagen hairs), together representing multiple independent probands with single-gene point variants. The remaining papers (fructose metabolism reviews, Tkfc promoter regulation, curcumin/MASLD, HCC biomarkers, structural and splicing studies) provide supportive biology but are not needed for the causal call. Given at least two independent human genetic studies with patient variants, Established is strongly favored, with a small residual for Existing if one considers phenotypic heterogeneity across reports.

Several of the listed articles use the homonym "CaV1.x" (voltage-gated calcium channels) and were dismissed (PMIDs 31355778, 31826954, 25107988, 27340545, 34261001). The core human genetic evidence is the rare variant burden analysis in enhancers identifying CAV1 as an ALS risk gene (PMID 33535055), supported by a large-scale follow-up in whole-genome sequencing, post-mortem RNA and iPSC datasets showing altered CAV1/CAV2 expression and enhancer-variant effects on survival/progression (PMID 36937187). Reviews list CAV1 among newly recognized ALS genes (PMID 37250416, 38239833), but these are citations of the same primary finding rather than independent replication in new probands/families, and the variants are regulatory/enhancer-level rather than clearly causal coding mutations. Strong supportive mechanistic and animal data (SynCav1 in hSOD1G93A mice; PMIDs 30894019, 35910808, 42614372) reinforce biological plausibility but are non-human. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with limited weight to "Established".

Only one human clinical report provides primary genetic evidence: PMID 31845315 describes a homozygous nonsense VPS26C variant (p.Glu60*) segregating in two affected cousins (a single consanguineous family) with neurodevelopmental deficits, growth failure, skeletal anomalies and dysmorphism, with supportive expression data. This is a single family/one report, so replication in independent probands is lacking, precluding "Established." Strong supporting biology exists: VPS26C is a Retriever/Commander subunit whose partners (VPS35L, CCDC22, WASHC5) cause Ritscher-Schinzel/3C syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMIDs 37172566, 40448120, 38062209, 38459129, 34943955), but these are structural/mechanistic or about other genes. Plant studies (29495075, 36618652) are non-human functional data only. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (if further probands are reported) and "Hypothesized."

The only human genetic evidence is a single three-generation Southern Chinese Han family with a heterozygous KCNAB3 H258R missense variant segregating with genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (PMID 32990398), a neurological/epileptic phenotype within the broader neurodevelopmental spectrum. This is a single proband family with no independent replication, so Established cannot be supported (only one qualifying PMID). Supporting evidence is functional/non-human: a knock-in adult mouse model characterizing the same mutation (PMID 36345448) and in vitro heterologous expression studies of Kvβ3/Kvβ1 subunits modulating Kv1 channel inactivation (PMIDs 8183366, 9857044), which establish biological plausibility but do not add human genetic replication. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the reliance on in vitro and mouse data.

Two primary human genetic reports present their own patient-derived variant data: PMID 27166630 describes a homozygous stop mutation in BOD1 co-segregating with intellectual disability in a large consanguineous (Iranian) family, with loss of mRNA/protein and supporting Drosophila learning/synapse phenotypes; PMID 32578875 reports an independent consanguineous Lebanese family with a homozygous nonsense variant (p.R151X) causing syndromic ID with dysmorphism, hearing impairment and gonadal dysfunction. These are two independent families with single-gene point variants, which supports Established, though the "syndromic" designation is only explicit in the second report and total human evidence remains limited (two families, no large cohort replication), which keeps Existing nearly as likely. Animal work (Bod1-deficient mice with autism-like and cognitive deficits, PMIDs 40164568, 39359881) and Drosophila knockdown provide strong supportive biology but cannot themselves raise the category. Other listed papers (COMPASS/AdipoRon metabolism, chromosomal aberration GWAS, bipolar twin WES) are peripheral co-mentions.

phenotype: microvascular complications of diabetes, susceptibility to, 6
justification: Two human case-control studies from the same Russian group (PMID 12815947 and its English companion PMID 14704872) report association of the SOD2 Ala(-9)Val (rs4880) polymorphism with diabetic polyneuropathy, a microvascular complication of type 1 diabetes — this is the primary evidence underlying the MVCD6 designation. However, these appear to derive from overlapping cohorts and thus do not constitute truly independent replication in separate probands or families, precluding "Established". A review (PMID 25512783) lists SOD2 among susceptibility genes for diabetic nephropathy, but this is background citation rather than primary evidence. Supporting mechanistic/animal data (PMID 40127616, proximal-tubule Sod2 knockout in Akita diabetic mice) is non-human and only supports the biological plausibility. Other listed articles concern unrelated phenotypes (glaucoma, Alzheimer's, sperm DNA fragmentation, COVID, prostate cancer) and are not relevant.

The only relevant article (PMID 33022222) reports human adRP families (RP17 locus) in which complex structural variants have breakpoints within a genomic interval spanning YPEL2 to LINC01476, so YPEL2 is positionally implicated in patients. However, these are multi-gene structural rearrangements that cannot single out YPEL2, and the authors' own functional data (Hi-C, iPSC-derived retinal organoids, qPCR) attribute the disease mechanism to neo-TAD formation causing ectopic retinal-enhancer contact and overexpression of GDPD1, not YPEL2. There is therefore no study demonstrating that YPEL2 sequence variants cause retinitis pigmentosa, precluding "Established". The remaining articles concern renal cell carcinoma, lymphoma, HBV integration and HIV viral load, and are irrelevant homonym/co-mention contexts. Evidence best fits "Existing" (human locus-level association) with substantial weight for "Hypothesized" (YPEL2 lies in a retinal-enhancer-rich TAD but is not the effector gene).

The clearest primary evidence is PMID 34636445, which reports a novel ATP5MC3 variant segregating in a single large pedigree with dystonia/spastic paraplegia, linked to chromosome 2q24-2q31 — one human family with a mitochondrial ATP synthase (complex V) subunit gene. PMID 34954817 reports patients with ATP synthase subunit variants causing variable neurologic phenotypes and may include additional ATP5MC3 probands, but the abstract does not explicitly confirm ATP5MC3 as one of the mutated subunits, so it cannot be counted with certainty as independent replication. PMID 36860166 (ATP5F1B dystonia) only restates the ATP5MC3 association as background, which is citation rather than new evidence, and PMID 42503482 uses ATP5MC3/SCMAS merely as a storage-material marker in CLN8 disease. PMID 41751777 is an unrelated hydrogel/tendinopathy study where Atp5mc3 is an incidental rodent expression readout. Given one definite human family plus a probable second cohort report, the evidence supports "Existing" most strongly, with meaningful but lesser probability for "Established".

Multiple independent human studies report MYH7 variants in probands and families with structural congenital heart disease, not merely cardiomyopathy. PMID 21127202 screened a population-based Ebstein anomaly cohort and identified MYH7 mutations; PMID 23956225 reports a family with Ebstein anomaly, VSD and LV hypertrabeculation with segregating MYH7 p.Glu1220del; PMID 35491958 describes three additional probands with 12 affected relatives with complex CHD/Ebstein anomaly; PMID 28864942 identifies a Dutch MYH7 founder variant associated with congenital heart defects; PMID 23117287 reports a novel MYH7 mutation in an infant with VSD and non-isolated LVNC. These are independent, single-gene (not CNV) human findings with familial segregation, satisfying replication. Remaining probability is assigned to "Existing" because much of the CHD spectrum is co-occurring with LVNC/cardiomyopathy and penetrance/phenotype boundaries remain debated.

Two independent human studies report NCOA3 missense variants segregating with autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss: a large Brazilian five-generation family (PMID 33326993, c.2810C>G, p.Ser937Cys, supported by linkage, exome sequencing, inner-ear expression, and a zebrafish ncoa3 knockout) and an Italian four-generation family (PMID 34356059, c.2909G>C, p.Gly970Ala), both variants in exon 15 with similar sensorineural phenotypes. This constitutes replication in two independent families, which supports Established, but the total evidence base remains small (two families, both authors describing NCOA3 as a "candidate"/"novel" gene), keeping Existing nearly equally plausible. All remaining articles concern unrelated NCOA3/SRC-3 biology (kidney disease, liver steatosis, cancer coactivator function, protein biophysics) and add nothing to the hearing-loss link. Hypothesized retains a small weight because much of the mechanistic support (zebrafish, mouse expression) is non-human, and Novel is essentially excluded.

Human variant-level evidence exists in more than one independent report: Knoll et al. identified LAMA4 mutations in cardiomyopathy patients with supporting functional work in cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells (PMID 17646580); a Chinese family showed a missense LAMA4 variant (p.G218R) segregating with DCM and conduction disease in three affected brothers (PMID 39686469); and a digenic LAMA4/MYH7 case of infantile DCM was reported (PMID 30650640). However, much of the remaining literature consists of LAMA4 variants of uncertain significance found incidentally in panel/exome screens (PMIDs 35284542, 25979592, 36317039, 31024045, 39272661) or in other phenotypes (ARVC, Fabry), and the strongest mechanistic support comes from Lama4-null mouse cardiomyopathy (PMID 16204254), which is animal rather than human evidence. One historical linkage study even excluded laminin-alpha4 as the candidate in a DCM family (PMID 11085912). Given the limited, partly digenic and VUS-laden human data with little independent replication of definitive pathogenicity, "Existing" is the most probable category, with a meaningful but smaller chance of "Established."

Two independent human reports provide primary genetic evidence: PMID 32631816 describes DLG5 variants in patients with multiple congenital anomalies including ciliopathy-spectrum features (renal, brain/hydrocephalus, and other cilia-related phenotypes) with supporting functional data, and PMID 30791088 reports a homozygous frameshift in DLG5 causing hydrocephalus and renal dysplasia, a classic ciliopathy-like presentation. These constitute at least two separate probands/families with single-gene point/frameshift variants, arguing for an Established relationship, though the total number of reported families remains small and one report is a single-family study, which keeps meaningful probability on Existing. PMID 35022528 mentions DLG5 only as an incidental finding in a Müllerian anomaly cohort (potential phenotype expansion), adding weak supportive but non-definitive evidence. The remaining articles concern DLG5 in inflammatory bowel disease, cell polarity, and cancer and are irrelevant to ciliopathy, although the polarity/scaffolding biology (PMID 24910533, 37001186) provides mechanistic plausibility underpinning the Hypothesized category.

Only one primary genetic study (PMID 33465109) reports a rare MAST2 Arg89Gln variant segregating with unprovoked venous thromboembolism in a single French family, supported by functional data (altered TFPI and SERPINE1/PAI-1 expression in endothelial and HEK293 cells). This is credible human evidence of a gene–thrombosis link, but it derives from a single family/proband without independent replication, so "Established" criteria (two or more independent probands/families in separate reports) are not met. The remaining articles concern MAST kinase biology, PDZ-domain peptide design, hearing loss, breast cancer, or antipsychotic metabolic effects, and do not add thrombosis-specific genetic evidence. A modest probability is retained for Established in case additional replication exists outside this list, and a small residual for Hypothesized given the mechanistic/in vitro nature of much of the supporting work.

Only one human genetic report (PMID 33359164) describes biallelic ETV2 variants (c.350del and c.757G>T) segregating with congenital heart defects, vertebral anomalies and preaxial polydactyly in four pregnancies of a single family; the authors themselves call it a "presumably novel gene-phenotype association" awaiting additional cases. A single family without independent probands cannot satisfy the replication requirement for "Established." The remaining literature is strongly supportive biologically — ETV2 as a master regulator of endothelial/hematopoietic specification in mice and zebrafish, links to NKX2-5, vascular development, and EndoMT in pulmonary hypertension (PMIDs 25722433, 29467221, 26396195, 36923254, 39391221) — but these are animal/in vitro data that support "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic evidence. Therefore the weight falls on "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized."

The original discovery paper (PMID 31051110) reports recurrent germline DLST mutations in multiple independent human probands with multiple pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas, including functional/segregation support, and a second independent human study (PMID 33180916) identified germline DLST variants in PPGL patients with associated epigenetic (hypermethylation) phenotypes. Additional human evidence includes a metastatic pheochromocytoma case with a rare DLST mutation (PMID 38835385) and a PGL case with a candidate DLST variant of uncertain significance (PMID 34877445), while PMID 37139660 provides mechanistic support (hyposuccinylation, metabolic remodeling) for pathogenicity. Reviews consistently list DLST among Krebs-cycle/pseudohypoxia PPGL susceptibility genes (PMIDs 32295730, 42626933, 36760809), though these are background citations rather than primary evidence. Because the number of independent probands is modest and some variants remain of uncertain significance (relatively common allele frequencies), a substantial probability remains for "Existing" rather than fully Established. Other listed papers concern Alzheimer's disease, cuproptosis, or non-human models and do not bear on this gene–disease link.

The only direct evidence is a single human study (PMID 32900841) delineating a new fibrillin-2-opathy and proposing a role for FBN2 variants in carpal tunnel syndrome pathogenesis, noting CTS heritability and familial clustering. No second independent report of FBN2 variants in CTS probands/families is present; the related paper on short stature, brachydactyly and joint contractures (PMID 40199564) describes an overlapping distal FBN2 phenotype but does not itself establish CTS causality. All remaining articles concern congenital contractural arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, bicuspid aortic valve, or incidental gene lists, which are background rather than replication for CTS. Because replication in independent human cohorts is lacking, "Existing" is the best fit, with limited weight to "Established" (if the fibrillin-2-opathy cohort itself contained multiple independent families with CTS) and to "Hypothesized" (fibrillin-2/microfibril biology in connective tissue of the carpal tunnel).

The only primary evidence is a single consanguineous Pakistani family (PMID 32778762) with a homozygous ~7.3 kb deletion that inactivates both MYADML2 and the adjacent PYCR1; the cutis laxa/connective-tissue features were attributed to PYCR1, with the skeletal anomalies speculatively assigned to MYADML2 by exclusion. Because the lesion is a contiguous multigene deletion in one family, it cannot isolate MYADML2 as the causal gene, so Established is essentially excluded (no two independent probands with gene-specific variants). It nevertheless constitutes a human genetic report proposing MYADML2 deficiency in a skeletal/connective-tissue phenotype, supporting Existing as the most probable category, with the authors themselves noting confirmation is needed. The MAL family review (PMID 38362940) is a cancer-focused overview and provides no relevant connective tissue evidence, leaving residual probability for Hypothesized (biology only) or Novel (all connective tissue features truly due to PYCR1).

No article in this set reports germline MAD1L1 variants segregating in prostate cancer families or in independent prostate cancer probands, so an Established call is not supportable. The closest human germline evidence is PMID 36360276, which used GWAS-catalog prostate cancer SNPs and network analysis to implicate MAD1L1 (alongside AR and CDKN1B) in ethnic differences in prostate cancer risk, and PMID 36322655, which shows biallelic germline MAD1L1 mutations cause a mosaic-variegated-aneuploidy-like syndrome with marked tumor susceptibility (though not prostate-specific and in a single female proband). Other prostate-relevant data are somatic: PMID 11423979 found MAD1L1 mutations in prostate cancer cell lines and tumors with dominant-negative checkpoint effects, and PMID 36922933 reported MAD1L1 somatic mutations in 13% of Nigerian prostate tumors—supporting tumorigenic relevance but not heritable familial risk. Much of the remaining literature concerns spindle-assembly checkpoint biology or unrelated phenotypes (colorectal cancer, PTSD, schizophrenia, HNSCC), which is mechanistic/incidental. Hence the weight is split between Existing (limited human germline association plus cancer-predisposition biology) and Hypothesized (checkpoint/aneuploidy mechanism plus somatic prostate findings).

phenotype: hypermetabolism due to uncoupled mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation 2
justification: None of the provided articles report ATP5PB (ATP synthase peripheral stalk subunit b) variants in patients with hypermetabolism due to uncoupled mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (Luft-type disease); there are no probands, families, or human genetic association studies, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The literature instead consists of expression/proteomic studies in cancer, macrophages, piglets, zebrafish, scallops, and cell lines showing ATP5PB/ATP5F1 changes with mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced ATP production (PMIDs 41714849, 37939958, 38159774, 42260326, 34575098). One study directly links ATP5PB allele frequency and expression changes to a chemical uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, but in sea lamprey, not humans (PMID 33767757), and MIPEP-related processing of ATP5F1 supports a role in respiratory chain function (PMID 42389375). This biology—ATP synthase subunit function and OXPHOS coupling efficiency—is directly mechanistically relevant to the phenotype, supporting a Hypothesized relationship rather than demonstrated genetic causation.

phenotype: joint contractures, osteochondromas, and B-cell lymphoma
justification: PMID 35789258 reports a single human proband with a homozygous germline NFATC2 frameshift (c.2023_2026delTACC; p.Tyr675Thrfs*18) presenting exactly with joint contractures, osteochondromas, and recurrent B-cell lymphoma, with functional/single-cell data supporting causality. This is credible direct human genetic evidence, but it is a single patient without independent replication in other probands or families, so "Established" cannot be met (only one qualifying PMID). Supporting but non-definitive human evidence comes from NFATC1/NFATC2 expression profiling in human osteochondromas (PMID 36747924), and strong corroborating animal/functional biology exists: Nfatc2-null mice develop ectopic cartilage/neoplastic chondrogenesis (PMID 10620601), Nfat1/Nfatc1-deficient mice develop osteoarthritis and osteophytes (PMIDs 19526482, 24248346), and NFAT1 roles in B-cell tolerance and germinal-center B-cell survival/BCL-6 signaling (PMIDs 16849457, 22124122, 15814705). Together this places the relationship firmly at "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (if the single-case report plus functional proof were judged sufficient) and for "Hypothesized" (if the single case is discounted as non-replicated).

Direct human genetic evidence exists: PMID 35438214 reports three unrelated probands with compound heterozygous DNAH14 variants (nonsense, frameshift, missense) and NDD phenotypes (seizures, global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia), and PMID 41596228 reports a novel homozygous truncating variant segregating in two siblings with neurodevelopmental features. However, the sibling report is confounded by co-occurring pathogenic FXN GAA expansions, and the authors themselves frame the DNAH14 contribution as possible rather than proven. PMID 36344539 lists DNAH14 only as a candidate ID gene of uncertain significance in a Middle Eastern cohort, which supports but does not confirm causality; PMID 26636390 implicates a DNAH14 deletion in familial panventriculomegaly, but a copy-number change cannot isolate the gene. Other listed papers concern PCD, sperm flagella, or circRNA cancer biomarkers and are not evidence for NDD causation. Overall the evidence is credible but limited/not definitive, favoring "Existing" with meaningful probability for "Established".

A single human case report (PMID 35112409) describes a de novo heterozygous nonsense NFE2L1 variant in a patient with developmental delay, hypotonia, hypospadias/bifid scrotum and failure to thrive, supported by in vitro dominant-negative functional evidence — credible but a single proband. A second report (PMID 41424762) only nominates NFE2L1 as a "potential candidate" disease gene from a splicing-prediction framework, which is suggestive rather than confirmatory, so replication in independent probands is lacking and Established cannot be supported. Much of the remaining literature concerns NFE2L1/NRF1 biology in proteostasis and its downstream role in other syndromes (NGLY1 deficiency, PSMC3-related deafness-cataract syndrome, Parkinson/Gaucher-related models), which provides strong mechanistic plausibility (hypothesized-level support) rather than direct variant evidence. Several listed papers use "NRF1/Nrf2" homonymously for nuclear respiratory factor 1 or NFE2L2 and are not relevant. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing".

PMID 35107634 reports two affected siblings from a single family with a homozygous frameshift variant (c.90dupC, p.Phe31Leufs*3) in C18orf32, supported by knockout/rescue experiments in HEK293 cells demonstrating loss of GPI-anchored protein processing — direct human genetic evidence for an inherited GPI deficiency disorder (GPIBD25). However, this constitutes only one family/proband report without independent replication in a second unrelated family, so the criteria for "Established" (at least two independent studies with patient variants) are not met. The second paper (PMID 41351175) concerns lipid droplet secretion and secretory autophagy and provides no patient variant data, contributing only supportive biology. Therefore the evidence is best classified as "Existing," with limited residual probability for "Established" should additional unlisted cohorts exist.

The only dedicated candidate-gene screen of LHX8 in POF patients (PMID 17624344) found only benign polymorphisms and no causal mutations, and reviews (PMIDs 34794894, 18574220, 17305537) list LHX8 among POI candidate genes largely on the basis of mouse oogenesis data rather than replicated human proband variants. Human genetic evidence does exist for a closely related ovarian phenotype: heterozygous loss-of-function LHX8 variants cause oocyte maturation arrest/female infertility (PMIDs 36029299, 41566502), and panel sequencing of POI cohorts has included LHX8 among mutated genes (PMID 27603904). However, oocyte maturation arrest is not identical to primary ovarian insufficiency, and I cannot cite two independent studies reporting LHX8 variants in POI probands with their own causal evidence, so "Established" is not supportable. Remaining support comes from animal/in vitro folliculogenesis work (PMIDs 36882745, 38181927), which underpins the "Hypothesized" tier. Overall, "Existing" best fits: credible but limited/indirect human evidence.

Direct human genetic evidence exists: PMID 35438214 reports three unrelated probands with compound heterozygous DNAH14 variants and NDD phenotypes (seizures, global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia), and PMID 41596228 describes two siblings with a novel homozygous truncating DNAH14 variant and neurodevelopmental/cognitive impairment, though this family also carries pathogenic FXN expansions, confounding attribution. PMID 36344539 lists DNAH14 only as an unconfirmed candidate gene among many in a consanguineous ID cohort, which is supportive but not definitive; PMID 30125339 similarly reflects candidate-level reanalysis. PMID 26636390 links a DNAH14 deletion to familial panventriculomegaly, but a copy-number deletion cannot isolate this gene. Remaining papers concern ciliary dyskinesia, sperm flagella, or circRNA cancer biomarkers and do not address neurodevelopment. Overall the evidence is credible but limited and not robustly replicated in unconfounded independent families, best fitting "Existing".

SLC11A1 (NRAMP1) is one of the classic human TB susceptibility loci, with numerous independent human case-control and family-based studies reporting associations of the (GT)n promoter repeat, INT4, D543N (rs17235409) and 3'UTR (rs17235416) variants with tuberculosis (e.g., 12447767 in a large case-control cohort, 35140349 in Pakistani patients, 37380553 in Warao Amerindians, 19193106 in Chinese pediatric TB, 34990850 in spinal TB, 15381817 in Malawi). Two large meta-analyses (16466030, 25856512) aggregate these independent datasets and confirm significant, replicated associations, and 12447767/35140349 additionally link the variants to functional consequences (IL-10 production, reduced SLC11A1 expression), supporting a mechanistic role. However, the evidence is that of a modest-effect susceptibility/risk locus rather than a definitively causal Mendelian gene, and several well-powered studies failed to replicate (12797705 in Morocco, 42470058 in southwestern China, 16637265 in Tuvinians), indicating population heterogeneity. This keeps the weight split between Established and Existing, with negligible probability for Hypothesized or Novel given the abundance of direct human genetic data.

Two independent human genetic studies report biallelic CCDC34 variants in infertile men with oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (spermatogenic failure 76): PMID 34348960 identified homozygous mutations in patients and corroborated causality with a mouse model, and PMID 38856307 reported a novel homozygous missense variant (p.A283E) in an unrelated consanguineous Pakistani family with matching flagellar/axonemal defects. These are separate probands from distinct populations, with functional and ultrastructural support, meeting the bar for replication in humans. Slight uncertainty remains because the total number of reported families is small and one report is a single-family missense variant, which is why some probability is retained for "Existing."

phenotype: congenital anomaly of kidney and urinary tract
justification: Only a single human report (PMID 37468454) describes a homozygous TBC1D31 missense variant segregating with CAKUT in three siblings of one consanguineous family, supported by in silico modeling; this is a single family without independent replication, so "Established" criteria (≥2 independent probands/families in separate studies) are not met. Supporting biological plausibility comes from PMID 33934390, showing TBC1D31 forms a centrosomal complex with praja2/PKA/OFD1 controlling primary ciliogenesis, with developmental defects in medaka — ciliopathy biology is highly relevant to renal/urinary tract malformation. The cancer-focused papers (PMIDs 39231952, 39206796) concern TBC1D31 as an oncogene/metabolic regulator and are not relevant to CAKUT. Thus evidence is credible but limited, best fitting "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single-family human evidence is deemed insufficient.

PMID 37315560 reports a de novo missense variant in IL1R1 (p.Lys131Glu) in a human patient with chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, with strong functional validation (loss of IL-1Ra binding, unopposed IL-1 signaling, patient PBMC inflammatory signatures, and a knock-in mouse recapitulating hyperinflammation and pathological osteoclastogenesis). This is credible, direct human genetic evidence, but it derives from a single proband in one report; no independent families or replicated probands are provided in this list. Other CRMO-related papers concern serum biomarkers (PMID 27000045) or IL1RN/DIRA variants (PMID 32259833), not IL1R1 variants, and remaining IL1R1 papers address unrelated phenotypes (celiac, ankylosing spondylitis, IgG4-RD, glaucoma, cancer). Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with limited probability for "Established" pending independent replication.

The only human study with sequence-level variants in GTF2IRD1 itself producing an NDD phenotype is the report of two brothers with biallelic missense variants in trans (PMID 36308390) — a single family, explicitly framed as a "possible novel disorder," which is insufficient for replication across independent probands. A de novo GTF2IRD1 variant was found in one childhood-onset schizophrenia proband (PMID 26508570), but it is listed only as a candidate among several genes. The remaining human evidence comes from atypical 7q11.23 deletions in Williams–Beuren syndrome (PMIDs 19568270, 23653586, 35379245, 36520254, 23118870), which are multigenic CNVs and cannot isolate GTF2IRD1 from neighboring GTF2I/BAZ1B, plus an imaging endophenotype SNP association (PMID 29884845). Strong supporting biology exists from mouse knockouts and forebrain organoids (PMIDs 22198572, 39671308, 17239664), which supports Hypothesized-level mechanism but not human causation. Overall, credible but non-definitive human evidence places this best in Existing.

The primary human genetic evidence comes from a single study (PMID 36670122), which reported a TWAS locus at NUP50 and a rare-variant burden association in 9,390 ALS/FTD patients versus 4,594 controls, plus a patient-derived frameshift carrier and supporting Drosophila/zebrafish loss-of-function models. This is credible human genetic evidence but has not been independently replicated in separate probands or families, so it falls short of "Established." Supporting but non-genetic human/animal work includes nucleoporin mislocalization (including NUP50) in SOD1 mice and sporadic ALS patients (PMID 28344074) and Nup50 mutation modifying TDP-43 neurotoxicity in flies (PMID 23468938), which would only support "Hypothesized" on their own. Other listed papers concern NUP50 cell biology, diabetes autoantibodies, pemphigus, or wasp QTLs and are not relevant to ALS causation; one dementia MR study links NUP50 to FTD risk, tangentially supportive given the ALS–FTD spectrum.

Only one primary article (PMID 36417180) reports pathogenic MPC2 variants in its own results—four patients from two unrelated families with homozygous c.148T>C (p.Trp50Arg) and c.2T>G (p.Met1?) variants causing an inborn error of mitochondrial pyruvate metabolism, with functional rescue in patient fibroblasts. The later case series/review (PMID 37899339) summarizes those same MPC2 cases as background (its own probands carried MPC1 variants), so it is a citation rather than independent replication. Other human genetic reports concern MPC1 variants (PMIDs 22628558, 34873722, 31145700) or a schizophrenia GWAS SNP (PMIDs 30087317, 27460766, 23933155), which does not support metabolic disease. Substantial supporting biology exists—MPC2 heterodimer structure/inhibition, TZD targeting, cardiac and hepatic stellate cell models, and MASH/diabetes relevance—but this is mechanistic/animal evidence. Because only a single primary human genetics PMID demonstrates causal MPC2 variants (albeit in two independent families), Existing is the most defensible category with meaningful probability for Established.

Only a single article in this list directly links MIR145 to multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome: PMID 36649075, reporting a seed sequence variant in miR-145-5p as causal. This is credible, human, and mechanistically plausible (miR-145 is a master regulator of vascular smooth muscle cell contractile phenotype, supported by PMIDs 38995239 and 30169548), but it constitutes a single report without independent replication in additional probands or families, so "Established" criteria (≥2 independent studies with patient variants) are not met. Other listed papers concern unrelated phenotypes (cancer, MDS del(5q), asthma, keratoconus, aging heart) or are homonym/incidental co-mentions and add no direct evidence. Supporting biology (miR-145 loss altering smooth muscle differentiation, aortopathy association in PMID 30059548) reinforces plausibility, keeping some weight on "Hypothesized" but the human causal report justifies "Existing" as most likely.

The decisive item is "Human MD2 deficiency—an inborn error of immunity with pleiotropic features" (PMID 36462957), which explicitly reports human LY96/MD2 deficiency as an inborn error of immunity; MD2 is the obligate TLR4 coreceptor, giving strong mechanistic plausibility. However, this is a single report and no second independent publication in the provided list describes additional unrelated probands or families with pathogenic LY96 variants, so criteria for "Established" (replication across independent kindreds) are not met. Supporting but weaker human genetic data include LY96 variants/polymorphisms associated with recurrent urinary tract infection (PMID 21390520), IBD susceptibility (PMID 24971461), infection outcome in trauma (PMID 26473437), and biologic treatment response in psoriasis (PMIDs 28696418, 37108492), which are immune-related but not IEI per se. Functional/animal and in vitro work (zebrafish Md-2, TLR4/MD2 signaling) supports biological relevance only. Hence "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability for "Established" if the MD2 deficiency paper describes multiple independent families.

Only one report (PMID 37461298) provides direct human genetic evidence: a homozygous TUFM variant (c.524G>C, p.Gly175Ala) in a single consanguineous family with premature ovarian insufficiency, supported by in vitro functional data and a Tufm variant mouse recapitulating POI. This is a single proband/family without independent replication, so the criterion of at least two independent human reports for "Established" is not met. Other TUFM literature concerns mitochondrial encephalopathy, mitophagy, NASH, aging, and viral immunity, and the 16p11.2 deletion paper (PMID 37834089) is a multigene CNV that cannot implicate TUFM specifically. Thus the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized" given the mitochondrial/folliculogenesis biology rationale.

phenotype: channelopathy-associated congenital insensitivity to pain, autosomal recessive
justification: The strongest evidence is a single human study (PMID 36454632) reporting two related affected individuals homozygous for a loss-of-function TRPV1 missense variant (N331K) with functional validation and clinical phenotyping showing capsaicin insensitivity and an elevated heat-pain threshold; PMID 40632671 is a commentary restating this same family rather than independent evidence. Because this constitutes one family/one report without independent replication in other probands, the criteria for "Established" (≥2 independent human studies with patient variants) are not met. Other listed papers concern TRPV1 biology, nociceptor function, animal models, or unrelated phenotypes (Alzheimer's, cannabinoid hyperemesis, body composition), and CIP-related papers implicate NTRK1 or PRDM12 rather than TRPV1 (PMIDs 22032467, 34646120, 21436684, 19482060). Thus the relationship is best described as "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (if the two individuals are treated as independent probands) and for "Hypothesized" (strong mechanistic/expression basis alone).

No article reports PLXNC1 variants in patients with cerebral cortical dysplasia or any malformation of cortical development, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The strongest relevant evidence is developmental neurobiology: PLXNC1 (with SEMA7A) participates in the induction–exclusion programs that pattern the cortical sensorimotor–association axis and mediates repulsive corticocortical axon guidance (PMID 42386980), and PLXNC1 acts as an R-Ras GAP regulating cell migration and neurite outgrowth (PMID 19136556), biology plausibly relevant to cortical patterning/migration defects. Other human genetic findings involve unrelated traits—language/reading ability (PMID 38538593), antidepressant response (PMID 29559929), frailty (PMID 42020437), DNA methylation and neighborhood deprivation (PMID 38663907)—none of which are precursors or subtypes of cortical dysplasia. Remaining papers concern immune, fibrotic, hematopoietic, and livestock growth phenotypes and are incidental co-mentions. Hence the relationship is best described as hypothesized on biological grounds, with substantial residual probability of being novel.

PMID 38592547 reports a single proband with compound heterozygous SUPT7L variants (missense causing aberrant splicing plus frameshift) presenting with generalized lipodystrophy and progeroid features, supported by patient fibroblast transcriptomics, DNA damage assays, and rescue by wild-type overexpression. This is credible human genetic evidence but derives from one individual only, with no independent replication in additional probands or families, so "Established" criteria (two or more independent reports) are not met. The other two articles (PMIDs 17967894, 24852358) concern STAF65γ/SUPT7L function in STAGA/Mediator-dependent MYC transcription and cancer, providing mechanistic background but no lipodystrophy link. Accordingly, the evidence best fits "Existing," with a small residual probability for "Established" if additional cases exist and a small allowance for purely mechanistic interpretation.

Two human genetic reports provide direct variant-level evidence: PMID 37833060 describes a homozygous founder variant in SGSM3 in Ashkenazi Jewish patients with an intellectual disability syndrome, and PMID 39390489 reports a novel homozygous stop-gain (p.Arg526Ter) in two siblings with short stature and ID from a different population, replicating the biallelic loss-of-function mechanism. This constitutes independent probands/families with single-gene point variants, which approaches "Established," but the second report is a single sibship and explicitly frames SGSM3 as a "strong candidate gene" requiring functional validation, so the evidence remains short of definitive replication. Supporting biology (PMID 17509819) shows SGSM3 modulates RAP/RAB small G-protein signaling and is expressed in CNS neurons, consistent with a neurodevelopmental role. Other papers (breast cancer association, C9orf72 transcriptomics, schwannomatosis candidate loci) are unrelated to ID and do not contribute.

phenotype: autosomal dominant medullary cystic kidney disease with or without hyperuricemia
justification: PMID 38096951 is the single primary human genetic study, reporting five families (two distinct missense variants, p.L66V and p.D33N) with autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease/medullary amyloidosis, with co-segregation in 48 genotyped individuals, elevated plasma ApoA4, and mass-spectrometry confirmation of mutant ApoA4 as the amyloid constituent — very strong causal evidence. However, the other supporting items (PMIDs 40835155, 42175989) are reviews that restate APOA4 as a known ADTKD gene rather than presenting independent probands, so replication across two independent primary reports is not documented in this list. Mouse/functional work (PMIDs 39699959, 33444292) supports the biological plausibility of ApoA4 amyloidosis in kidney but is non-human. The remaining articles concern lipid/triglyceride traits and are irrelevant to this renal phenotype. Hence the weight is split between Established and Existing, favoring Existing slightly under the two-primary-study requirement.

Only one article (PMID 38627542) provides direct human genetic evidence: a single large three-generation Chinese family with acrokeratoelastoidosis (Costa type, classified as punctate palmoplantar keratoderma type III) linked to chromosome 12 and carrying a CCDC91 splice mutation (c.1101+1G>A), supported by knockdown/knockout functional work showing impaired tropoelastin transport. This is credible but derives from a single kindred without independent replication in other probands or families, so the criterion of at least two independent causal reports is not met, placing the evidence at "Existing" rather than "Established." The remaining papers (hip geometry, OPLL, DISH, lung function, white matter microstructure, pig litter traits) associate CCDC91 with unrelated skeletal, pulmonary, neural, or livestock traits and contribute nothing to the dermatologic phenotype. A small residual probability is retained for "Established" should the family-based linkage plus functional validation be judged definitive, and for "Hypothesized" if the human evidence is considered too preliminary.

The strongest evidence is PMID 38272662, which reports two unrelated female probands with de novo heterozygous missense CELSR1 variants causing fetal pleural effusions and progressive hydrops, supported by in vitro functional assays showing disrupted localization, junction formation, and PCP signaling. This is a single publication, however, so independent replication in a second cohort is not clearly documented; PMID 36959127 addresses the genetics of fetal lymphatic anomalies (hydrops, chylothorax) but the abstract does not explicitly confirm CELSR1 findings. Supporting, mechanistically relevant human evidence links CELSR1 variants to primary/hereditary lymphedema and lymphatic valve dysfunction (PMIDs 26855770, 37225411, 35948757, 37232218), a lymphatic developmental defect strongly related to nonimmune hydrops. Other papers (spina bifida, CADASIL, Phelan-McDermid deletions, mouse PCP studies) are either about different phenotypes or involve multigene deletions and do not isolate CELSR1 for hydrops. Overall this best fits "Existing" with a substantial but minority chance of "Established."

Two independent human clinical/genetic studies report their own patient cohorts with biallelic CIAO1 variants: PMID 38950322 (with its preprint PMID 38196629) describes patients with biallelic loss-of-function CIAO1 variants causing a neuromuscular/CNS phenotype with functional validation and lentiviral rescue, and PMID 38411040 independently reports inherited cytosolic Fe-S assembly disorders due to CIAO1 (and MMS19) deficiency with a lethal neurodegenerative phenotype — the disorder catalogued as multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome 10. Additional human reports support this, including a homozygous CIAO1 missense variant arising through maternal uniparental isodisomy 2 (PMID 40935480) and a commentary/report on CIAO1 mutations causing neuromuscular deficits (PMID 40047889). Mechanistic and model-organism work (PMIDs 40196589, 40924805, 41131702, 39011897) corroborates that patient variants (e.g., R65W) disrupt CIA targeting-complex client recruitment and Fe-S enzyme maturation, matching the disease mechanism. Evidence is therefore replicated in independent human probands with strong functional support, supporting "Established," with residual probability for "Existing" given the relatively recent and small number of reported families.

None of the provided articles report CCT7 variants in patients with a complex neurodevelopmental disorder. The only human genetic study (PMID 24213632) links a CCT7 missense variant to myocardial infarction via soluble guanylyl cyclase, a cardiovascular rather than neurodevelopmental phenotype, and the follow-up zebrafish work (PMID 33716783) is likewise vascular. The nearest neurological relevance is indirect and in vitro: the CCT3/CCT7 apical domains inhibit tau aggregation in neurodegenerative (not neurodevelopmental) disease models (PMID 40400346), CCT7 transcript changes under oxidative stress in dopaminergic cells (PMID 17397968), and yeast/Candida studies of chaperonin folding of actin/tubulin (PMIDs 20600117, 21209325), which give a faint mechanistic plausibility for neuronal cytoskeletal folding. This supports at most a weak hypothesized link, with the balance favoring Novel since the co-mentions are largely incidental to neurodevelopment.

Only one report (PMID 38041405) provides direct human genetic evidence: a heterozygous missense MARK4 variant (p.Phe202Leu) in two affected siblings inherited from a mosaic mother, with functional gain-of-function assays showing increased tau phosphorylation and mTORC1 signaling. This is a single family/one segregating variant, so it does not meet the threshold of multiple independent probands or families required for "Established." Supporting biological plausibility comes from tau kinase biology, mTOR pathway regulation, synaptic/mitochondrial roles in Drosophila (PMID 37550059), mouse tauopathy models (PMID 38712317), and a de novo MARK4 variant in early-onset Alzheimer disease (PMID 26194182), but those concern neurodegeneration rather than neurodevelopment. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with some residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the single-family report is judged insufficiently definitive.

The strongest evidence is PMID 41260215, which reports 26 independent families (35 individuals) with bi-allelic loss-of-function PRMT9 variants causing a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder, with functional support in patient fibroblasts and a zebrafish knockout — this alone constitutes multiple independent probands. PMID 38561334 provides corroborating human-variant evidence by functionally characterizing an intellectual-disability-associated PRMT9 missense variant (G189R) showing loss of methyltransferase activity, plus a conditional knockout mouse with impaired synapse development and learning, though its own results are largely mechanistic rather than a new clinical cohort. PMID 25712083 lists PRMT10 (a PRMT9 alias) among genes implicated in autosomal-recessive cognitive disorders and finds association with intelligence, adding supportive human genetic context. PMID 30679813 concerns FBXO11, which historically carried the "PRMT9" alias but is a distinct gene, and is dismissed as a homonym; cancer, Parkinson's, cardiac, and C. elegans/biochemistry papers are not directly relevant to Mendelian NDD causation. Because independent clinical replication essentially rests on a single (large, multi-family) report, some probability is retained for "Existing".

The only variant-level evidence linking CCT4 to a neurological phenotype comes from the spontaneous rat mf mutation (Cct4 1349G>A, C450Y) causing hereditary sensory neuropathy (PMID 12874111, 15193290), and that same study explicitly failed to identify CCT4 mutations in human HSN patients; the human chaperonin disease gene is CCT5, not CCT4 (PMID 16399879). Biochemical work characterizing the C450Y CCT4 subunit is in vitro (PMID 25124038), and other supporting data are model-organism or cell-based (Drosophila TOR/organ growth, PMID 30792539; CCT-dependent autophagy and polyQ/huntingtin aggregation, PMIDs 27929117, 24298020, 30488434), plus mouse expression changes in an Alzheimer's model (PMID 34959983). This constitutes plausible, directly relevant biology (proteostasis, actin/tubulin folding, neurodegeneration) but no human genetic evidence for a complex neurodevelopmental disorder, and the animal phenotype is a sensory neuropathy rather than a neurodevelopmental disorder. Remaining papers concern cancer or generic chaperonin biochemistry and are not phenotype-relevant. Therefore Hypothesized is by far the best fit; Established is excluded since no human proband/family studies can be cited.

The strongest evidence is PMID 42168171, which reports twelve patients with a homozygous intragenic loss-of-function copy number variant (IRAK2-Δex2) presenting with autoantibody production, gastrointestinal ulceration, recurrent infection and an elevated type I interferon signature, with mechanistic validation (failed IRAK4 interaction, impaired Myddosome/NF-κB signaling) in patient cells, knock-in mice and knockout lines; because the deletion is confined to IRAK2, it does isolate this gene. PMID 39299377 independently describes two additional patients with novel IRAK2 mutations causing impaired TRAF6 modification and defective TNF-α production, supporting causality in separate probands. These are reinforced by multiple human genetic association studies linking IRAK2 variants to SLE (31650390), rheumatoid arthritis (29129009, 35588430), and Hashimoto's disease (31073143), plus functional variant work (24662294, 24973222, 26250868) showing altered NF-κB/TLR signaling. Some uncertainty remains because the definitive monogenic cohort derives largely from one report and the second report emphasizes infection susceptibility rather than autoimmunity, so a substantial share of probability is retained for "Existing." Papers on stroke-heart syndrome, MPN transcriptomics, T1D linkage and the 3p25.3 multigene duplication are incidental or non-gene-specific.

The single available article (PMID: 38641995) reports biallelic loss-of-function variants in ZFTRAF1 in humans causing a neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and hypotonia, which is direct human genetic evidence of causality. However, only one publication is provided, so the requirement of at least two independent articles reporting probands/families for "Established" is not met. The evidence is credible and likely multi-family within that single report, but replication across independent publications is lacking, making "Existing" the most appropriate category. Hypothesized and Novel are nearly excluded because direct patient variant data exist rather than merely biological plausibility or incidental co-mention.
