The only human genetic evidence linking ATP6V1C1 to a neurodevelopmental phenotype is PMID 39210597, which reports a single individual with DOORS-like features caused by a dominantly acting ATP6V1C1 variant, supported by functional studies showing gain-of-function upregulation of V-ATPase activity and lysosomal/autophagy defects. This is a single proband, not replicated in independent families, so the "Established" threshold (two or more independent probands/families with single-gene variants) is not met. The other human ATP6V1C1 variant report (PMID 41539473) concerns non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss rather than a neurodevelopmental disorder, though it reinforces pathogenicity of missense variants in this gene. Remaining papers provide supportive biology (V-ATPase lysosomal acidification, bone/craniofacial and mouse models) consistent with a "Hypothesized" underpinning, but the paralogous ATP6V1B2 precedent for ZLS/DOORS/DDOD strengthens plausibility. Overall, "Existing" best describes credible but limited human evidence.

The only direct human genetic evidence is PMID 38411040, which reports the first inherited disorders of the cytosolic Fe-S protein assembly system and explicitly describes MMS19 deficiency producing a lethal neurodegenerative phenotype in patients. This is a single report, so replication across independent publications with patient-derived MMS19 variants is not demonstrated; the companion paper (PMID 38950322) concerns CIAO1, a different gene of the same CIA targeting complex, and thus supports the pathway but not MMS19 itself. Extensive supporting biology exists (MMS19 as core CIA targeting-complex component delivering Fe-S clusters to DNA repair/replication enzymes, iron homeostasis regulation via FBXL5, proteostasis effects) but these are yeast, plant, worm, or in vitro studies and would only justify "Hypothesized" on their own. Given one credible human clinical study plus strong mechanistic plausibility, "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability for "Established" if that report contains multiple independent families.

Two entries (PMID 38633811 and PMID 39698362) report essentially the same study, in which whole-genome sequencing of sporadic cystic kidney disease patients identified rare missense CFAP47 variants in three unrelated males, with supporting cilia expression data and a knockout mouse showing tubular dilation. This is credible human genetic evidence, but it is a single primary report rather than independent replication across multiple studies, so it falls short of "Established." All other listed papers concern CFAP47 in sperm flagella, asthenozoospermia, PCD, or comparative genomics, or involve a large multigene Xp21 deletion, and thus do not add independent kidney-specific evidence. The mouse knockout data alone would only support "Hypothesized," but the human proband variants push the weight toward "Existing."

Two human reports directly link KAT2B variants to SRNS: PMID 39366742 describes the first family (two siblings) with a KAT2B loss-of-function variant causing early-onset SRNS with bilateral cataract, and PMID 29768408 reports a homozygous KAT2B variant in a family with ADD3 deficiency where SRNS and cardiomyopathy were present, supported by Drosophila nephrocyte and human podocyte functional data. However, the second report frames KAT2B as a modifier/susceptibility gene acting together with ADD3 rather than an independent monogenic cause, so replication of a clear causal role in independent probands is not firmly established. The remaining articles concern cancer, obesity, congenital heart disease, autophagy or other unrelated contexts and do not bear on SRNS. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a substantial but minority probability for "Established," and a small residual for "Hypothesized" if one considers the causal human evidence limited to functional/model support.

The strongest human evidence is a single report (PMID 36384317) identifying rare damaging missense and splicing variants in AFDN in African nsCL±P case-parent trios with a Brazilian whole-exome replication cohort, plus computational support for disrupted interactions with nectins/CDH1. This is credible but constitutes one primary study rather than multiple independent replicated clinical reports, so Established is unlikely. Supporting biology comes from mouse work showing palatal epithelial loss of Afdn causes highly penetrant cleft palate via the nectin–afadin axis (PMID 32554531), which is animal data and thus underpins Hypothesized rather than human causality. Other listed articles concern AF-6/afadin cell-junction biology, PDZ interactions, cancer, or tethered cord syndrome and are not cleft-specific genetic evidence. Overall, Existing best describes the current state of evidence.

The only human variant-level evidence directly relevant to an inborn error of energy metabolism is PMID 39401966, describing a single proband with a homozygous ME2 frameshift (p.Phe460fs*22), neurodevelopmental disorder, dilated cardiomyopathy and lactate elevation, with functional support (unstable protein, yeast complementation). A single family/proband, explicitly framed as "candidate" and requiring confirmation, cannot satisfy the requirement for two independent probands/families, so Established is unlikely. Additional human genetic data (ME2 haplotype association with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, PMIDs 15532013, 16190936) concern a neurological complex trait rather than an energy-metabolism disorder, though they support that ME2 variation has phenotypic consequences in humans. Extensive functional and animal work (mitochondrial NADPH/NADH production, TCA flux, mitobiogenesis, CoA-binding mouse mutants with mitochondrial dysfunction; PMIDs 33770508, 42094367, 33554057, 37079187) firmly establishes biological plausibility, supporting a substantial residual weight for Hypothesized.

Only one primary clinical genetics report (PMID: 39638757) provides patient-level evidence: biallelic LRRC45 variants (a splice variant and a missense) in three individuals from two unrelated families with severe CNS anomalies, supported by patient fibroblast studies showing aberrant splicing, reduced LRRC45 protein, and impaired ciliogenesis. This is credible human genetic evidence but constitutes a single study proposing a novel disorder, without independent replication in a separate publication. The functional work on LRRC45 in ciliogenesis (PMID: 30131441) and the ciliopathy cohort study (PMID: 34716235) provide supportive biological plausibility rather than independent variant-level proof. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with some probability for "Established" given that two unrelated families with functional validation are described within that report.

The strongest human evidence is a single case report of compound heterozygous loss-of-function BMP5 variants in a patient with skeletal dysostosis, dysmorphism and atrioventricular septal defect (PMID 39239663) — one proband, not replicated. Supporting but weaker human data include a rare BMP5 splice-region variant in monozygotic twins with microtia (PMID 34183628, effectively one family, and a craniofacial rather than classic skeletal dysplasia phenotype) and dysregulated BMP5 expression (not variants) in a child with axial skeletal malformations and heterotopic ossification (PMID 17345627). Additional human associations concern osteoarthritis/bone mineral density (PMIDs 28764194, 25030405, 37830501), which are related skeletal traits but not dysplasia. Robust mechanistic and animal support exists (short-ear mouse Bmp5 nonsense mutation with skeletal element defects, PMIDs 7958439, 9081658, 35765140), which underpins biological plausibility but is non-human. Because fewer than two independent human probands/families with BMP5 variants causing skeletal dysplasia are demonstrated, "Existing" is the best fit.

All provided articles concern ZBTB40 in the context of bone mineral density/osteoporosis GWAS loci (PMIDs 30661131, 19801982, 24249740, 32497039, 30013441, 25771420) or male infertility/spermatogenesis in mice (PMID 37174664). None report neurodevelopmental phenotypes, cognitive/behavioral outcomes, or brain expression relevant to neurodevelopmental disorder. There are no human probands or families with ZBTB40 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorder, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. A small residual weight is given to Hypothesized because ZBTB40 is a BTB-zinc-finger transcriptional regulator with roles in chromatin/DSB repair and telomere biology in mice, biology that could in principle be relevant to neurodevelopment, but no such link is demonstrated here.

The only direct human genetic evidence for CNKSR1 itself is a single Iranian consanguineous family with a novel frameshift variant causing syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability, supported by loss of transcript/protein in patient lymphoblastoid cells and Drosophila cnk knockdown brain phenotypes (PMID 30450701). A second cohort study lists CNKSR1 among genes only "very rarely" linked to microphthalmia (PMID 29450879), which is a different phenotype and not independent replication for neurodevelopmental disorder. Most remaining papers concern the paralog CNKSR2 (a well-established X-linked ID gene) or generic KSR/RAF-MAPK scaffolding biology, and cannot be credited to CNKSR1. Since only one proband family with a point/frameshift variant supports causation, the criteria for Established (≥2 independent probands/families in separate reports) are not met, leaving Existing as the best fit, with some residual weight on Hypothesized given the reliance on model-organism and MAPK-pathway biology.

Multiple independent human studies report USP27X variants in probands with X-linked intellectual disability: PMID 25644381 originally identified USP27X as a novel XLID gene through X-exome sequencing with co-segregation analysis in unrelated families; PMID 38182161 reports 10 new XLID105 individuals from nine additional families with biochemical evidence that variants disrupt USP27X deubiquitylating activity and protein interactions; PMID 39007861 describes two further affected males with a previously unreported pathogenic variant; and PMID 40596734 adds another proband with a missense variant supported by in vitro functional data. These constitute replicated, gene-specific (non-CNV) evidence in humans across independent probands, with a defined OMIM entity (XLID105, #300984). Supporting functional/methodological papers (PMID 39400174) and related DUB-module work (PMID 38753057) reinforce biological plausibility, while PMID 38273165 mentions USP27X only incidentally.

Three independent reports present their own patient-derived evidence of biallelic COQ5 variants causing a neurodevelopmental phenotype: PMID 29044765 describes three siblings (Iraqi-Jewish family) with intragenic biallelic COQ5 duplications, cerebellar ataxia, encephalopathy, seizures and cognitive disability with reduced CoQ10; PMID 37599337 reports a fifth patient from a third family with a novel c.681+1G>A and recurrent p.Gly118Ser variant, defining a core phenotype of intellectual disability, encephalopathy and developmental delay; PMID 41199775 adds two further siblings with compound heterozygous frameshift and missense variants, supported by yeast complementation showing loss of function. These are independent probands/families with intragenic variants, satisfying replication for causality in humans. Supporting mechanistic and pathway data (COQ5 C-methyltransferase in CoQ10 biosynthesis, CoQ10 deficiency neuroimaging reviews, yeast/Drosophila models) reinforce biological plausibility but are not required for the established call. A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" given the very small total number of reported cases.

None of the supplied articles mention schizophrenia or any psychiatric phenotype; they concern the SLC4 family of cation-coupled bicarbonate transporters in kidney, epididymis, salivary gland, eye and inner ear, plus blood-pressure salt sensitivity. No human genetic association study links SLC4A8 variants to schizophrenia, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The only tenuous biological rationale is that NDCBE (SLC4A8) regulates neuronal intracellular pH and excitability and is expressed in brain, and the SLC4 family is implicated in epilepsy and drug addiction (PMID 25428855, 18577713), which could underpin a hypothesized mechanism, but this is not articulated toward schizophrenia in any cited work. Consequently the evidence is best described as Novel, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on the transporter's neuronal pH-regulatory biology.

Only one article (PMID 26881968) presents primary human genetic evidence, reporting two deaf children each carrying two WBP2 variants, alongside a mouse model showing progressive high-frequency hearing loss and inner hair cell afferent synapse defects. This is a single credible study rather than replicated independent clinical reports, so the criteria for "Established" (at least two independent human studies with variants in probands/families) are not met. The remaining supportive data are murine (PMID 42531911, showing Wbp2 mutant hearing loss modified by Cdh23ahl) or purely biochemical/oncologic (WW-domain, YAP/TAZ, ITCH, Dyrk1b papers), which support biological plausibility rather than human causation. Therefore "Existing" is most probable, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single human report is judged insufficient, and a small chance additional replication exists to justify "Established".

Most MYBPC3 literature concerns hypertrophic cardiomyopathy rather than congenital heart disease, but several human studies do report MYBPC3 variants in CHD probands: a large exome study of 5,424 CHD probands found enrichment of rare damaging recessive genotypes in contractility genes including MYBPC3 in left-sided CHD (PMID 40030011); a familial ASDII sarcomere screen identified an MYBPC3 A833T variant in two unrelated ASD subjects (PMID 22194935); a heterozygous Mybpc3 mutation was reported with bicuspid aortic valve (PMID 33209723); and candidate variants appear in VSD trio and single-ventricle WES analyses (PMIDs 31440271, 41153298). These reports are suggestive and involve independent human probands, yet they are small, largely candidate/computational, and none provides definitive replicated causal proof for CHD specifically, so "Established" is not warranted. Supporting mechanistic human tissue data (reduced cMyBP-C in CHD fetuses, PMID 28315668) reinforces biological plausibility but is functional rather than variant-based, keeping some weight on "Hypothesized."

Three independent human clinical genetic studies report biallelic DDX59 variants in patients with orofaciodigital syndrome, a recognized ciliopathy spectrum disorder: PMID 23972372 identified distinct homozygous DDX59 variants in two multiplex consanguineous Arab families with linkage and exome data; PMID 28711741 reported a novel homozygous stop-loss variant in three probands from two unrelated South Asian families; and PMID 29127725 described a homozygous frameshift (p.Phe62fs*13) with functional evidence of impaired SHH signaling in patient-derived cells. These are point/small variants in independent probands from separate research groups, satisfying replication requirements. Supporting mechanistic work (Drosophila mahe, PMID 32072499; nuclear RNA pathway screen, PMID 40399278) reinforces biological plausibility, including minor intron retention in OFD-associated genes. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" given that ciliogenesis appeared intact in mutant fibroblasts, leaving some debate about whether DDX59-related OFD is a canonical ciliopathy.

Human genetic evidence exists but is not replicated at the causal level. PMID 23473037 reports a single family carrying a SIRT1 L107P mutation in which affected members developed type 1 diabetes or ulcerative colitis, with functional support (NO, cytokine, chemokine overproduction) — this is one proband/family only. PMID 24570024 shows SIRT1 promoter polymorphisms (rs3758391) act as modifiers of SLE morbidity (nephritis, SLEDAI) rather than susceptibility, and PMID 34269838 associates SIRT1 SNPs with corticosteroid sensitivity in primary immune thrombocytopenia, another autoimmune disorder. These are credible but limited/non-replicated human association studies, supported by strong mechanistic and animal work (EAE astrocyte Sirt1 knockout, PMID 36136587; immune-regulatory reviews PMIDs 22105513, 33330467, 34689102). Because no two independent studies demonstrate causal variants in separate probands/families, "Existing" is the most appropriate category.

Multiple independent human reports identify biallelic IARS2 point mutations in patients with Leigh syndrome. The original description (PMID 25130867) reported compound heterozygous IARS2 mutations in a patient with Leigh syndrome; PMID 30041933 reported novel compound heterozygous IARS2 variants in two Japanese siblings with Leigh syndrome/West syndrome; PMID 35228874 described an additional independent proband with compound heterozygous p.Val499Glyfs*14 and p.Arg784Trp presenting with Leigh disease; and PMID 39169373 provides further patients plus functional evidence of combined OXPHOS deficiency. A Korean cohort of Leigh syndrome patients (PMID 32020600) also identified IARS2 among causative nuclear genes, supporting replication across independent populations. These are separate probands with single-gene-resolving variants, satisfying the criteria for an established gene–disease relationship.

None of the provided articles mention Tourette syndrome or any tic disorder; the literature is dominated by cancer biology (esophageal carcinoma, del(5q) myeloid neoplasms, colorectal cancer predisposition, renal cell carcinoma splicing), RNA-binding biology, and unrelated neurological contexts. The only neuro-adjacent reports concern hnRNPA0 co-localization with tau inclusions in tauopathy (PMID 30068389), allele-specific binding at a late-onset Alzheimer's HLA locus (PMID 35341343), and a rare-variant exome study of suicide/asthma pedigrees (PMID 25335167) — none of which involve Tourette syndrome or a recognized precursor of it. These give at most a weak, generic rationale that HNRNPA0 is a neuronally expressed RNA-binding protein, insufficient even for a hypothesized link to tics. No human genetic variants in HNRNPA0 have been associated with Tourette syndrome in this evidence set, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

phenotype: short stature and microcephaly with genital anomalies
justification: Only one clinical report in the list (PMID 29228025) describes a biallelic CENPT defect in two affected siblings from a single consanguineous family with severe primordial growth failure, supported by patient cell lines and a zebrafish Cenpt knockdown model. This is credible human genetic evidence but derives from one family/one report, with no independent probands replicating the finding, so it falls short of "Established" (which requires at least two independent human reports). The remaining articles are purely mechanistic studies of CENP-T in kinetochore assembly, centromere chromatin, and chromosome segregation in yeast, chicken DT40, insects, and human cell lines, which support biological plausibility (mitotic/kinetochore dysfunction causing microcephalic primordial dwarfism) but provide no patient variants. Hence the bulk of probability goes to "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single-family report is judged insufficient.

None of the provided articles address neurodevelopmental phenotypes. The HIVEP1 literature here concerns NASH/TH17 immunometabolism in mice (PMID 41124285) and interaction of the HIVEP1 splice variant Cirip with Cirhin in North American Indian childhood cirrhosis, a hepatic cholestatic disease (PMIDs 18021715, 19732766). No human genetic variants in HIVEP1 are reported in probands or families with complex neurodevelopmental disorder, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. A small residual weight for Hypothesized reflects the gene's role as an NF-κB-related transcription factor important in development, which could in principle offer an indirect biological rationale, but there is no direct neurodevelopmental relevance in these papers.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebellar hypoplasia and spasticity
justification: Only one primary human genetics study (PMID 28542170) reports biallelic INTS8 variants (compound heterozygous 9-bp deletion and splice-altering missense) in a single family of three affected siblings with severe neurodevelopmental delay and neuronal migration defects, supported by functional work showing disrupted Integrator complex stability and UsnRNA misprocessing. A single family, even with multiple affected siblings, does not constitute independent replication, so Established cannot be supported; no second primary proband/family report is present in this list. Other papers merely cite INTS8 as background (PMID 30683929 lists it among PNH genes; PMID 31428919 mentions it only via interaction networks) or address unrelated biology, such as Drosophila neural progenitor studies (PMID 31018143), PP2A recruitment mechanisms (PMID 32966759), and cancer somatic mutation surveys (PMIDs 28468258, 26536348). The strong, directly relevant mechanistic and model-organism data support a residual weight on Hypothesized, but the existence of credible human variant evidence makes Existing the most probable category.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic MRPS23 variants in patients with combined oxidative phosphorylation/respiratory chain deficiency: Kohda et al. first identified MRPS23 as a novel causative gene in a childhood-onset respiratory chain complex deficiency cohort (PMID 26741492); a subsequent cohort reported five independent probands (eight homozygotes) with the founder variant c.119C>T p.P40L showing combined complex I and IV deficiency in fibroblasts (PMID 38086984); an adult leukoencephalopathy series reported biallelic pathogenic MRPS23 variants with impaired mitochondrial translation and multiple OXPHOS defects (PMID 41506652); and proteomic profiling reclassified an MRPS23 VUS as pathogenic by demonstrating loss of mitoribosomal subunits (PMID 39288270). These are human, independent probands/families with gene-level (not CNV) variants plus supporting functional biochemistry, satisfying replication. Remaining probability mass goes to Existing because much of the strongest cohort evidence relies on a single founder allele in one ethnic group. Cancer/expression papers (PMIDs 33927350, 35962848, 42593047, 32987154, 28957804) are not relevant to disease causation here.

phenotype: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 21 with or without anosmia
justification: The primary evidence is Miraoui et al. (PMID 23643382), which sequenced FGF8-synexpression genes in 386 CHH probands and identified FLRT3 mutations in 3 individuals, but explicitly framed these as contributors to an oligogenic architecture rather than monogenic causes. A second human report (PMID 37108593) describes a previously reported heterozygous FLRT3 variant (p.Ala369Val) in a cHH patient, again in an oligogenic context and without functional proof of causality. Other listed papers (PMIDs 25071724, 24456696, 39327214, 31200363) merely restate FLRT3 as a known CHH candidate gene as background rather than presenting new probands, and thus count as citations, not replication. Remaining articles concern FLRT3 biology in synapses, angiogenesis, and mouse development (PMIDs 22405201, 18448090, 26235031), which support biological plausibility but not causation for HH21. Given the limited, non-definitive, largely oligogenic human genetic evidence, "Existing" best describes the relationship, with limited weight on "Established."

Multiple independent human genetic studies provide primary evidence: PMID 34707297 reports ten novel patients from eight families with truncating/missense ITSN1 variants (7/14 de novo) presenting autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy; PMID 38346866 is an independent case report of a de novo pathogenic ITSN1 variant with autism, regression and absent speech; PMID 35982159 identifies ITSN1 at exome-wide significance in 42,607 autism cases through de novo and inherited LoF variants; and PMID 33994118 independently prioritizes ITSN1 among candidate NDD/ASD genes in a Chinese cohort. These are independent probands/cohorts with single-gene resolution (not multigene CNVs), satisfying the replication requirement. Supporting mechanistic data from Itsn1/2 knockout mice showing ASD/OCD-like behaviors and cortico-striatal deficits (PMID 37603735) reinforce plausibility, while the Parkinson's disease haploinsufficiency findings (PMID 40056900) indicate variable expressivity rather than weakening the NDD link. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the effect size is moderate and penetrance/expressivity is variable.

The CLPB literature consistently supports a different phenotype: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type VII with cataracts, encephalopathy, movement disorder, intellectual disability and congenital neutropenia (PMIDs 25597511, 34140661, 34115842, 26916670, 37906145), and none of the provided papers report Leigh syndrome or Leigh-like basal ganglia lesions attributable to CLPB variants in their own results. The only Leigh-specific item is a GeneReviews overview of nuclear gene-encoded Leigh syndrome spectrum (26425749) that is co-listed but provides no CLPB-specific proband data, and the WES diagnostic cohort (27290639) does not explicitly attribute Leigh syndrome to CLPB. Biologically, CLPB is a mitochondrial disaggregase whose loss disrupts mitochondrial proteostasis and OXPHOS-related function (32573439, 35499078, 35328774), a mechanism plausibly overlapping the Leigh syndrome spectrum, which supports a Hypothesized-level relationship. Because no independent human probands with Leigh syndrome and CLPB variants are documented here, Established is excluded and Existing is only weakly supported by generic mitochondrial-encephalopathy overlap.

Human genetic evidence directly links biallelic TNK2 variants to early-onset epilepsy: PMID 23686771 reported a homozygous missense variant segregating in a consanguineous family with infantile-onset epilepsy plus functional data (loss of NEDD4 binding/degradation), PMID 27977884 described two additional patients with TNK2 mutations and late-onset infantile spasms, PMID 39493104 reported a further biallelic TNK2 epilepsy case (explicitly the fourth), and PMID 42407302 identified TNK2 among genes in a DEE cohort. These are independent probands/families with single-gene point variants, which supports replication for an epilepsy phenotype. However, the reported phenotype is severe autosomal recessive infantile-onset epilepsy/developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with intellectual disability, not classical genetic generalized epilepsy, and the original authors themselves noted that definitive proof of pathogenicity awaits confirmation. Remaining papers concern oncology, virology, lupus, and Parkinson's biology and are irrelevant or homonymous, so the balance favors "Existing" with substantial probability for "Established".

The only direct human genetic evidence linking IFT74 to isolated spermatogenic failure comes from a single study (PMID 33689014, with its correction PMID 33770252) reporting two unrelated infertile men with a homozygous IFT74 missense variant (c.256G>A) causing MMAF/asthenozoospermia without syndromic ciliopathy features, supported by functional splicing and sperm flagellar localization data. This is credible, human, proband-level evidence, but it derives from one publication rather than multiple independent replicating clinical studies, so "Established" cannot be justified under the stated rule. Other IFT74 papers describe Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Joubert syndrome, or skeletal ciliopathies (PMIDs 32144365, 33748949, 33531668, 34539760, 37555648, 37315079), which support the biological plausibility (motile cilia/flagellar assembly, tubulin transport, subfertility in mice) but do not directly address spermatogenic failure in humans. Therefore the weight falls on "Existing", with residual probability on "Established" (two unrelated probands within the one study) and "Hypothesized" (strong flagellar biology and animal data).

phenotype: epilepsy, early-onset, with or without developmental delay
justification: Two articles present primary human genetic evidence linking SETD1A variants to early-onset epilepsy: PMID 31197650 reports four missense SETD1A variants (three de novo, one segregating in a four-generation family) in children with early-onset epilepsy, with supporting neuronal functional assays, and PMID 37928142 describes an independent de novo frameshift variant (p.Glu1002Glyfs*20) causing infantile epileptic spasms syndrome with developmental delay. These are independent probands from separate groups, which supports Established; however, the first study's variants are missense of uncertain pathogenicity in a gene whose established mechanism is loss of function, and the second is a single case report, so the evidence is thinner than for the well-replicated SETD1A neurodevelopmental/schizophrenia syndrome (PMIDs 26974950, 32346159), where seizures are not a core reported feature. Other cited works (speech disorder, autism, schizophrenia, methylation episignature) support a broad neurodevelopmental role but restate rather than replicate the epilepsy association. Accordingly, probability is split between Established and Existing, with little weight on Hypothesized or Novel.

Human genetic evidence for ILK in DCM comes primarily from one study (PMID 17646580), which reported ILK missense mutations (e.g., p.P70L) in human dilated cardiomyopathy with supporting functional work in zebrafish and endothelial/cardiomyocyte models. A second human genetic study (PMID 30802431) identified de novo/damaging ILK variants in two unrelated families, but with an arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy phenotype, while re-citing the earlier DCM variant as background rather than reporting new independent DCM probands; overlapping cardiomyopathy phenotype supports but does not replicate DCM causation. The remaining supportive literature is animal/in vitro: cardiac-specific ILK ablation causing DCM and heart failure in mice (PMID 16951252), ILK-deficient zebrafish msq mutants (PMID 30463267), rat overexpression models (PMID 22348065), PINCH knockout mice (PMID 19652092), and mechanotransduction/SERCA2a mechanistic work (PMID 25208486); expression studies in failing human hearts (PMIDs 21625516, 17131835) are correlative, not genetic. Because at most one human study provides primary variant-level DCM evidence, "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability for "Established" given the closely related cardiomyopathy family findings.

Human variant-level evidence exists in more than one primary report: PMID 34092786 describes six subjects from four unrelated families with de novo or segregating rare PRICKLE2 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift) presenting global developmental delay, autistic features, ADHD and epilepsy; PMID 23711981 reports two ASD probands with rare inherited PRICKLE2 missense variants supported by functional assays; and PMID 21276947 identified epilepsy patients with heterozygous PRICKLE2 mutations alongside fly/mouse seizure models. However, the evidence is tempered by inherited variants from unaffected fathers, small cohorts, and an explicit rebuttal (PMID 26942291) questioning PRICKLE2 involvement in epilepsy, with the rebuttal exchange (PMID 26942292) underscoring ongoing controversy. Additional support is largely mechanistic/animal (PCP–PSD-95 synaptic biology, Prickle2-null mouse ASD-like behaviors, USP9X interaction, new patient-derived iPSC lines), which strengthens plausibility but does not by itself establish causation. Overall the literature best fits a credible but not yet definitively replicated gene–disease relationship, leaning between Existing and Established.

Nearly all the retrieved articles use "GATC" as a DNA sequence motif (Dam methylation/mismatch repair recognition site) or refer to bacterial gatC of the galactitol PTS, and are therefore homonym hits irrelevant to the human GATC gene. The single genuinely relevant article (PMID 30283131) reports nine patients from five families with pathogenic variants in the GatCAB complex subunits QRSL1, GATB and GATC causing a lethal mitochondrial cardiomyopathy, with functional evidence (deficient mt-tRNAGln aminoacylation, impaired mitochondrial translation, lentiviral rescue, yeast modeling). This is credible human genetic evidence directly linking GATC to an inborn mitochondrial metabolism disorder, but only a subset of those families carried GATC variants, and no independent replicating publication is present in this list. Per the stated criterion requiring at least two independent publications with patient variants for "Established," the evidence best fits "Existing," with some residual probability that the multi-family report plus subsequent literature would qualify as Established.

Only one primary human genetic study (PMID 30085091) reports a homozygous HKDC1 missense variant (c.173C>T, p.T58M) in two unrelated families with late-onset retinal degeneration, supported by absence in controls, reduced hexokinase activity, retinal expression, and an Hkdc1 knockout mouse with RP-like phenotype. A second paper (PMID 41187334) is an enzymology study that characterizes the same RP-associated T58M variant in vitro, showing a modest 2-fold reduction in catalytic efficiency — functional support, but not independent patient/family evidence. All other listed papers concern hepatic metabolism, gestational hyperglycaemia, cancer, keratoconus, or lysosomal biology and are irrelevant to RP causation. Since only a single publication reports probands, replication in independent clinical studies is lacking, so "Existing" best describes the evidence, with residual probability for "Established" (two unrelated families within that one report) and "Hypothesized" (much of the mechanistic support is murine/in vitro).

Two human studies report NEBL variants directly in cardiomyopathy patients: Purevjav et al. (PMID 20951326) identified four nebulette variants (K60N, Q128R, G202R, A592E) in patients with DCM/endocardial fibroelastosis, and PMID 27186169 screened cardiomyopathy cohorts and reported NEBL mutations across DCM and other cardiomyopathy phenotypes. However, much of the supporting evidence is functional/animal (transgenic and knockout mice, PMIDs 23632046, 25987543, 33861145, 27733623), and the one dedicated human genetic-association study (PMID 11140941) found the actin-binding-motif polymorphism associated only with non-familial idiopathic DCM, explicitly not with familial IDC. Reviews (PMIDs 26321576, 36935760) restate the association as background rather than providing independent probands, so replication across independent families with clear segregation is not convincingly demonstrated. This pattern—credible but limited and partly disputed human evidence bolstered by strong mechanistic models—best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" and "Hypothesized."

Only one article in this list reports its own patient-level genetic findings for SLC51A: PMID 36148443 describes two siblings and a second cousin with reduced OSTα (SLC51A) expression, fat malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and mild liver/cholestatic involvement — a single kindred, not independent replication. Other papers either restate SLC51A as a known PFIC gene in background (PMID 39143102, 37697751) or concern the partner subunit SLC51B/OSTβ (PMID 28898457), which supports the pathway but does not establish SLC51A itself. Substantial supportive but non-human/in vitro evidence exists (Ostα-knockout mice with altered bile acid handling and cholestasis, structure–function and structural studies noting disease-associated mutations: PMIDs 19902485, 22542490, 35462858, 29420067, 34599072, 41606314), which underpins strong biological plausibility. Because credible human genetic evidence exists but lacks demonstrated independent replication in these articles, "Existing" is most likely, with meaningful residual probability for "Established" given the gene is the recognized cause of PFIC6.

Only one primary clinical genetics study (PMID 30085091) reports HKDC1 variants in patients: a homozygous missense variant (c.173C>T, p.T58M) segregating in two unrelated families with late-onset autosomal-recessive retinal degeneration, supported by reduced hexokinase activity and a Hkdc1 knockout mouse recapitulating RP-like phenotypes. A second paper (PMID 41187334) biochemically characterizes the RP-associated T58M variant, but this is in vitro functional support rather than independent patient ascertainment, so it constitutes replication of function, not of clinical association. Since I cannot cite two independent primary clinical reports of probands/families, the evidence falls short of Established and best fits Existing (one credible human genetic study with limited replication). Remaining literature on HKDC1 concerns glycemia in pregnancy, liver metabolism, cancer, and neurodegeneration, providing biological plausibility but no additional retinal-disease variants.

Only one primary human genetic report links CALCRL to this phenotype: PMID 30115739 describes a single consanguineous case of nonimmune hydrops fetalis with lymphatic dysplasia caused by a homozygous in-frame V205 deletion in hCALCRL, supported by in vitro trafficking/signaling assays and lymphatic-endothelial Calcrl and Ramp2 knockout mouse models that phenocopy NIHF. This provides credible but single-family, non-replicated human evidence, so "Established" cannot be supported (no second independent proband/family report is present in this list). The remaining articles concern CALCRL/CLR–RAMP pharmacology, AML biology, migraine/erenumab response, glaucoma (RAMP2), and unrelated obesity SNPs, which are not evidence for lymphatic malformation 8 but do support biological plausibility (adrenomedullin–CLR–RAMP2 axis in lymphangiogenesis). Hence "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on Established (strong functional corroboration) and Hypothesized (much of the mechanistic support is animal/in vitro).

Two independent human genetic studies report biallelic loss-of-function variants in STK33 in infertile men: PMID 34155512 identified a novel homozygous frameshift (c.1235del, p.T412Kfs*14) in four affected brothers of a Pakistani family with asthenozoospermia/MMAF, and PMID 37146716 identified two loss-of-function (frameshift and nonsense) mutations in seven individuals with non-obstructive azoospermia, with knock-in/knockout mouse modeling and phosphoproteomic substrate identification (AKAP3/4) supporting causality. Supporting biology includes testis-enriched expression (PMID 16176263), interaction with germ cell proteins TSKS/YBX2 (PMID 39909973), and pharmacologic inhibition phenocopying the infertility phenotype in mice (PMID 38781365). This constitutes replicated, gene-level (single-nucleotide/indel, not CNV) human evidence in independent probands/families, meeting the Established threshold; some residual probability is kept for "Existing" given the modest number of reported families. Unrelated homonym/other-phenotype papers (e.g., suicide-risk review) were not used as support.

Only one primary human genetic study (PMID 35142290) reports a novel heterozygous missense variant (c.2812G>A) in ZNF862 co-segregating with autosomal-dominant HGF in a single four-generation Chinese family, supported by functional data showing increased COL1A1 synthesis. PMID 38482719 provides only in vitro mechanistic support in human gingival fibroblasts (p21-RB1, Bcl-xL-Caspase 3 pathways), which strengthens biological plausibility but does not add independent patient variant evidence. PMID 35665929 merely restates the ZNF862–HGF association as background while reporting different candidate genes (ALK, CD36), so it counts as citation rather than replication. With only one independent family/proband cohort, the evidence is credible but not replicated, placing this at "Existing" rather than "Established".

The primary evidence is a single human study (PMID 36399538) reporting compound heterozygous loss-of-function GTF3A variants in one patient with common variable immunodeficiency and herpes simplex encephalitis, supported by functional work showing impaired HSV-1-induced innate immunity and loss of RNA5SP141/RIG-I signaling. PMID 36477413 is a commentary/highlight restating this finding rather than independent evidence. The recent cohort of ten patients with biallelic GTF3A variants (PMID 42428087) establishes TFIIIA deficiency as a cause of (S)CID with T cell lymphopenia, but does not report HSE probands, so it does not replicate the HSE association directly (though immunodeficiency is a plausible risk context). The IBDV proteomics paper (PMID 39442197) is incidental co-mention in chicken cells. With only one independent human proband for HSE, "Existing" is the best fit.

A single human study (PMID 36657711) reports a novel heterozygous nonsense VEZF1 variant (p.Lys164*) segregating with autosomal dominant DCM in one family, absent from 200 DCM patients, 400 controls and population databases, with functional luciferase assays showing loss of transactivation of MYH7 and ET1 promoters. This is credible but single-family, non-replicated evidence, so it cannot meet the "Established" bar requiring at least two independent probands/families from separate reports. Supporting biology is strong but non-human: Vezf1 knockout/knockdown mice show impaired cardiac structure and contractile function (PMID 31911272), and Vezf1 regulates endothelin-1 and vascular development (PMIDs 11504723, 15882861, 20431070). Remaining papers are mechanistic or unrelated phenotypes (cleft palate, nuchal translucency, KLF bioinformatics). Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single family report is discounted.

Only one clinical report (PMID 38432637) describes a human patient—a single pediatric proband with a homozygous RAB35 missense variant (p.R27H) causing global developmental delay, hydrocephalus and Dandy-Walker malformation—supported by functional evidence of loss of Rab35 activation, Arf6 dysregulation, and abnormal cytokinesis/primary cilia. This is credible but constitutes a single proband without independent replication, so "Established" cannot be supported (a second independent patient/family report is absent). Substantial supporting biology exists: Rab35 regulates neurite outgrowth, synaptic vesicle recycling, myelin growth via mTORC1, and mouse knockout causes embryonic lethality and developmental defects (PMIDs 38530365, 32503983, 28129039, 25694427), which underpins a plausible mechanism but is animal/in vitro. Other papers concern LRRK2-mediated Rab35 phosphorylation in Parkinson's disease, cancer, or infection and are not relevant to neurodevelopmental disorder causation. Thus "Existing" is the most probable classification, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single case is considered insufficient.

The only human report directly linking SERPINA11 variants to hydrops fetalis is a single case (PMID 40406169) with a homozygous SERPINA11 variant, but it is confounded by co-existing Rhesus alloimmunization and compound heterozygous PIEZO1 variants (PIEZO1 being an established nonimmune hydrops gene), so the SERPINA11 contribution is not isolated. PMID 38831697 reports a biallelic loss-of-function SERPINA11 variant in two fetuses from one family with a perinatal lethal extracellular-matrix phenotype plus mouse/HEK293T functional support, but this is a single family and the phenotype is not clearly hydrops fetalis. PMID 28749478 lists SERPINA11 only as a novel candidate gene of uncertain significance in a molecular autopsy cohort. Thus there are not two independent human probands with hydrops attributable specifically to SERPINA11, precluding Established; the evidence best fits Existing (one credible but limited human report) with meaningful weight on Hypothesized given the reliance on candidate-gene and functional/animal data.

The discovery study (PMID 34788392) identified an NPTX1 missense variant (p.G389R) segregating in a large family and then found the same variant in four additional unrelated families without a shared founder haplotype, plus a second variant (p.E327G) in a fifth family, with supporting functional work (ER stress, ATF6, loss of secretion). Independent human replication follows: a de novo missense variant in infantile-onset cerebellar ataxia (PMID 35560436), a de novo variant in a late-onset ataxia patient (PMID 35285082), an Indian case of SCA50 with an NPTX1 mutation (PMID 42241187), and phenotype expansion with dystonia/brain iron accumulation in NPTX1-SCA50 (PMID 40956878). The gene is now formally designated SCA50/NPTX1 in authoritative reviews of dominant ataxias (PMID 37479376). Other listed papers concern NPTX1 as a CSF/synaptic biomarker or unrelated biology and do not affect this judgment. Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands and families, supporting an Established relationship.

Only one report (PMID 35485770) describes a human genetic variant in NRG1 — a rare homozygous missense variant in a single family with mixed axonal/demyelinating neuropathy, with partial loss of function shown in zebrafish; the authors themselves call this "tentative," and no independent replication in other probands is present. The 8p12-p21.2 interstitial deletion case (PMID 16528753) spans 42 genes and cannot implicate NRG1 specifically. The remaining literature is strong biological/mechanistic support in animal and in vitro models — NRG1 type I driving onion bulb formation and CMT1A-like neuropathy in mice (PMID 30931926), NRG1-ErbB signaling in Schwann cell myelination and sensory neuropathy (PMIDs 14555954, 36314052, 28261057), and NRG1 modulation in diabetic neuropathy models (PMIDs 36218239, 32920546) — which supports a Hypothesized floor but not human causality. Therefore Existing is the most probable category, with Hypothesized as the main alternative and Established very unlikely given the lack of two independent human families.

Human genetic evidence links TRIM47 to cSVD markers: the CHARGE GWAS identified the chr17q25 locus containing TRIM47/TRIM65 for white matter hyperintensity burden (PMID 21681796), and a large gene-mapping study of extreme cSVD reported a probably damaging common missense variant in TRIM47 with supporting Mendelian randomization and expression data (PMID 35511193); TRIM47 also appears among replicated WML loci in Japanese GWAS (PMID 39537646). However, these are common-variant association findings in population cohorts, not causal variants segregating in independent probands or families, so the "Established" bar (at least two studies with patient-level causal variants) is not met. Functional support is largely non-human or in vitro (endothelial knockdown, Trim47-deficient mice, KEAP1/NRF2 pathway; PMIDs 41667829, 25586835), which reinforces plausibility but counts toward Hypothesized rather than Established. Papers on TRIM47 in cancer or norovirus (PMIDs 33833824, 36906594, 41251344, 42292357) are irrelevant to the phenotype.

The only direct evidence linking MCF2L to vascular malformation is a single human exome sequencing study (PMID 36760094) reporting candidate variants in three of seven families with a distinct systemic artery–to–pulmonary artery (aneurysm) malformation, explicitly framed as a "novel candidate disease gene" pending functional validation. This is one report rather than replicated independent studies, so it supports "Existing" rather than "Established." Supporting but indirect human vascular evidence includes a rare functional MCF2L variant co-segregating with premature atherosclerosis with impaired Rac1/RhoA activation and MCF2L protein in atherosclerotic lesions (PMID 25898923), and MCF2L nomination as an endothelial-cell CAD locus in a multimodal atlas (PMID 42245058), consistent with a vascular endothelial/cytoskeletal role. Other papers concern osteoarthritis, bladder cancer, neuroblastoma, keratoconus, or a multigene 13q34 deletion (PMID 26645620), which cannot isolate MCF2L. Functional Dbl/Dbs studies (PMIDs 12637530, 10523665) provide only mechanistic plausibility.

One human case report describes a patient with compound heterozygous ATG9A mutations presenting with autophagy-associated immune dysregulation and lymphoid hyperplasia, including EBV-related and CBM-signaling immune abnormalities (PMID 35838483) — a single proband, which supports "Existing" but falls short of the replication in independent families required for "Established". The remaining supportive evidence is mechanistic or murine: ATG9A loss in mouse keratinocytes causes TNF/STING-driven inflammatory skin disease and interferonopathy-like features (PMIDs 41118755, 36520901, 37014272), and ATG9A participates in innate immune/antimicrobial pathways (PMIDs 40259479, 39768205), which underpins the "Hypothesized" allocation. Other human variant reports for ATG9A concern ovarian insufficiency and early-onset Parkinson disease rather than immunodeficiency (PMIDs 30224786, 42327715), and several papers only co-mention ATG9A as an autophagy cargo/target. Thus the evidence is credible but limited to a single human proband plus strong immune-relevant biology.

The only direct human genetic evidence comes from a single consanguineous Pakistani family in which the DFNB44 locus was mapped (PMID 15583425) and subsequently a homozygous nonsense variant ADCY1 c.3112C>T (p.Arg1038*) was identified by exome sequencing (PMID 24482543). These two papers describe the same family, so there is no independent proband or family replication required for "Established". The same study provides strong supporting functional data (zebrafish adcy1b morphants with hair cell dysfunction, mouse inner ear expression/localization), which reinforces biological plausibility but is non-human. All other listed articles concern unrelated phenotypes (pain, cognition, epilepsy, cancer, liver disease) or are homonym/incidental co-mentions. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing", with limited probability for "Established".

Only one primary human study (PMID 36564894) provides original genetic evidence: biallelic PPCDC variants (p.Thr53Pro, p.Ala95Val) in two affected sisters (a single family) with fatal cardiomyopathy, supported by absent PPCDC protein, reduced CoA, and yeast functional assays. The other supporting articles (PMIDs 36983025, 42601840) are reviews that restate this finding as background rather than reporting independent probands, so they count as citations, not replication. Without at least two independent primary reports of patient variants, the criteria for "Established" are not met, though the functional depth and clear mechanism make the association credible. Remaining PPCDC papers concern yeast, plant, bacterial, or Drosophila enzymology, or a blood-pressure eQTL analysis, which support biological plausibility only.

The primary evidence is a single study (PMID 36972684) that identified functional DAAM2 mutations in patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome and demonstrated mechanistically that DAAM2 polymerizes nuclear actin at the androgen receptor to drive AR-dependent transcription. This is credible human genetic plus functional evidence, but it is one report and I cannot cite a second independent study reporting DAAM2 variants in separate AIS probands or families. The follow-up myosin VI paper (PMID 41443423) and the cryptorchidism pilot study (PMID 42677286) restate the AIS association as background or test previously characterized variants in a different phenotype, so they constitute citation/extension rather than independent replication. Other DAAM2 papers concern nephrotic syndrome, bone mineral density, schizophrenia and Wnt signaling, which are unrelated phenotypes. Therefore "Existing" is most appropriate, with modest weight on "Established" given the strength and functional depth of the Nature report.

Only one primary human clinical report demonstrates causality: a single Dutch proband with compound heterozygous SLIRP variants (frameshift plus deep-intronic splicing) causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with complex I and IV deficiency, supported by rescue experiments in patient fibroblasts (PMID 34426662). No second independent proband or family is reported in this set, so the "Established" threshold of at least two independent human genetic reports is not met. Other references to "pathogenic SLIRP mutations" (e.g., PMID 39087558) are background citations within mouse/Drosophila functional studies, not independent patient evidence. Extensive supporting biology (LRPPRC–SLIRP complex, mitochondrial mRNA stability and translation, knockout mice, Drosophila and C. elegans models) reinforces plausibility but is non-human, favoring "Existing" with residual weight on "Hypothesized".

phenotype: congenital anomaly of kidney and urinary tract
justification: Direct human variant-level evidence exists: Weber et al. (PMID 18305125) reported three SIX2 mutations in patients with renal hypodysplasia with supporting zebrafish functional assays, and Hwang et al. (PMID 24429398) independently identified a heterozygous SIX2 mutation in 1 of 650 CAKUT families; a further cohort reported a SIX2 variant in a patient with renal and skeletal anomalies (PMID 34122504). However, replication is weak and contested — a dedicated resequencing study of 125 CAKUT patients found no SIX2 variants and concluded routine testing is unwarranted (PMID 22809486), and PMID 24429398 explicitly noted that several previously reported CAKUT mutations are likely benign variants. Other supportive material is non-human/developmental (Six2+ nephron progenitors, mouse models: PMIDs 37772431, 32226308, 30377232) or concerns non-renal SIX2 deletion phenotypes (PMIDs 26581443, 27383657), which cannot count toward causality for CAKUT. The balance therefore favors "Existing" with meaningful but not definitive probability of "Established".

Only one article (PMID 37046053) directly reports NALCN variation in temporal lobe epilepsy: a father with drug-resistant temporo-orbitofrontal epilepsy and his son with mild temporal epilepsy, both carrying a likely pathogenic intragenic deletion of exon 27. This is a single family in a single report, without independent replication, so it cannot satisfy the requirement of at least two independent probands/families demonstrating causation. Other NALCN literature describes IHPRF1 (biallelic LOF) and CLIFAHDD (GOF) with hypotonia, developmental delay, and generalized/polymorphic seizures (PMIDs 29399786, 30167850, 24075186), supporting plausible epileptogenic biology through impaired regulation of resting membrane potential and neuronal excitability, but not temporal lobe epilepsy specifically. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (if the family report is deemed sufficient combined with broader epilepsy phenotypes) and "Hypothesized" (if the single case report is discounted and only mechanistic/general-epilepsy links remain).

The only human genetic evidence linking PHF10 to a multiple congenital anomaly/dysmorphic phenotype comes from terminal 6q27 deletion syndrome, where PHF10 lies within the minimal critical region alongside DLL1, THBS2 and C6orf70/ERMARD (PMIDs 24736736, 24056535, 39106599). These are multigene contiguous deletions, so they cannot single out PHF10, and indeed the functional follow-up implicated C6orf70/ERMARD rather than PHF10, with in utero Phf10 silencing in rat producing only mild migration delay and no heterotopia (PMID 24056535) — animal-level evidence supporting a Hypothesized role. No study reports intragenic PHF10 point mutations in independent probands with a dysmorphic/congenital anomaly syndrome, so Established cannot be supported. Remaining literature concerns cancer biology, PBAF complex structure and neural chromatin remodeling (PMIDs 35477757, 19561591, 38033872), which provides plausible developmental biology but no patient variant data. Hence points are split mainly between Existing (candidate gene in a human deletion syndrome) and Hypothesized (biology/animal data only).

Multiple independent human case-control studies report associations between TLR4 coding variants (Asp299Gly/rs4986790, Thr399Ile/rs4986791) and IBD: PMID 15194649 (Asp299Gly with both CD and UC), PMID 15207785 (Thr399Ile with UC), PMID 16010583 (A299G enriched in Dutch CD), PMID 27107867 (Brazilian CD phenotypes) and PMID 27069792 (rs4986791 in Malay CD). Two large meta-analyses (PMID 30617966 of 49 case-control studies; PMID 26089865; also PMID 26023918) confirm significant, replicated associations, particularly in Caucasians. However, several well-powered cohorts found no association (PMID 15190267 Scottish/Irish, PMID 22219617 Korean, PMID 17914947 New Zealand), and the effect sizes are modest risk-modifying rather than clearly causal, and TLR4 is not a genome-wide-significant, universally replicated IBD locus. Therefore the evidence is best described as a robust but non-definitive association (Existing), with substantial weight also given to Established given replication across independent probands and meta-analytic support.

None of the provided articles reports hydrocephalus as a phenotype in patients or animals with VPS50 variants; the human VPS50 disorder is characterized by severe developmental delay, postnatal MICROcephaly, hypoplastic corpus callosum, seizures and neonatal cholestasis (PMIDs 34037727, 38876772), which is not hydrocephalus and in fact the opposite head-size direction. The only potentially supportive human finding is a rare VPS50 mutation associated with neural tube defects (PMID 30828385); NTDs such as myelomeningocele are a well-recognized precursor/risk factor for hydrocephalus, which gives partial weight to "Existing," though this link is indirect and unreplicated. Remaining evidence is biological/animal (mouse brain deletion affecting synaptic function, Drosophila EARP/GARP trafficking in neuronal morphogenesis; PMIDs 38926759, 36239632), which supports at most a "Hypothesized" relationship involving endosomal trafficking in neurodevelopment. No article demonstrates a causal VPS50–hydrocephalus link in independent probands, so "Established" is excluded, and a substantial probability remains that the co-mention is incidental (Novel).

Only one article in this list directly addresses the bent bone dysplasia phenotype: PMID 33242826, which reports biallelic LAMA5 variants identified by exome sequencing in patients with a distinct bent bone skeletal dysplasia, supported by functional work on focal adhesion/WNT signaling and cell migration. This is credible human genetic evidence but represents a single report, so replication in independent probands or families is not demonstrated within the provided literature. All other LAMA5 papers concern unrelated phenotypes (nephrotic syndrome/glomerulopathy, congenital myasthenic syndrome, epilepsy, multisystem connective tissue syndrome, metabolic traits), which support LAMA5 as a broadly pathogenic basement-membrane gene but do not confirm the bent bone dysplasia association. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with only limited weight for "Established" given the lack of a second independent clinical report.
